articles.title: ‘Chemsex’ then and now – towards a ‘6Ws’ model for functional analysis and configurational assessment that embraces phenotypic diversity
articles.authors: Stephen Naulls
articles.abstract:
Background: Distinguishing problematic from non-problematic chemsex, or placing experience on a continuum of severity, generates limited information about why similar drug use can lead to different experiences and support needs. We propose considering how the circumstances of an encounter work together and change over time.
Method: This think piece presents a selective conceptual synthesis of chemsex research and assessment approaches, informed by minority stress theory, drug, set and setting, functional analysis, and addiction science. Empirical studies inform the domains and the proposed relationships between them.
Results: Six questions (who, what, why, with, where and when) describe the person, substances, functions, relationships, settings and timing within a changing chemsex configuration. Digital activity may connect these through partner contact, planning and support, and is an important emerging consideration. Three fictional vignettes illustrate different responses to comparable exposure. The person and therapist could each map the configuration, compare accounts and identify a focus for formulation and therapy.
Conclusions: Assessment should determine how pleasure, protection and harm arise through interacting circumstances. The six Ws direct attention to these relationships and to differences between the person’s and therapist’s accounts. Participatory development and longitudinal evaluation are needed to establish whether this approach improves shared understanding, decisions and care.

articles.title: LifeDive: Cross-kingdom phenotype estimates for 35,856 species
articles.authors: Tyler Maxwell Moore
articles.abstract:
Dense, standardized species-by-trait matrices support comparative biology and ecology, but their
coverage remains uneven. LifeDive uses a general-purpose, web-search-enabled language model
within a scripted annotation pipeline to estimate traits across animals, plants, and fungi. The
workflow assembled 35,856 species by 196 phenotype questions, yielding 7,027,776 entries in a
completed matrix; 16.6% of entries were imputed from other machine-derived annotations. Four
ordered substantive responses express model judgments about trait statements, with a separate
code for unknown or inapplicable cases. An exploratory 14-factor representation summarized broad
biological contrasts, although statistical factor-retention criteria suggested substantially more
dimensions. A benchmark screened 168 external criteria, with selected results reported for 44;
many biologically direct associations were strong, particularly for taxonomy and selected ecological
traits. A separate model-assisted audit reported 96.5% directional agreement in a selected
taxonomy-rule subset and approximately 237 agreements among 240 selected species-specific
checks. These audit subsets do not estimate accuracy across the whole matrix, and the
AmphiBIO-derived benchmark results require qualification because unrecorded categories were
treated as negative indicators. Trait profiles also produced recognizable taxonomic and functional
groupings. LifeDive offers a broad computational phenotype resource for exploration, hypothesis
generation, and prioritizing expert review. Individual values remain estimates, and downstream
inference requires attention to imputation, sampling, source dependence, and trait-specific
verification. The reported application programming interface and computing expenditure was
approximately US$10,000.

articles.title: Rapid processing deficits in children with dyslexia: Influence of stimulus, modality, and genes of interest
articles.authors: Tracy M Centanni Rosen; Vishal J Thakkar; Logun PK Gunderson; Remington Crossnoe; Abby S Engelhart
articles.abstract: Rapid automatized naming (RAN) performance is highly predictive of reading outcomes when administered prior to the start of formal reading instruction. Children with dyslexia struggle with this task and RAN difficulties are described as a main deficit in this population. Perhaps unsurprisingly, some children with dyslexia also exhibit deficits in rapid auditory temporal processing of tones. Given that automaticity tasks rely on speed, the goal of the current study was to evaluate rapid processing tasks, their relationship to RAN, and associated genetic variants of interest. Children with or without dyslexia completed an assessment battery, provided a saliva sample for genotyping, and completed self-paced tasks of rapid auditory and visual perception online. Children with dyslexia were significantly slower to respond during tasks that included a linguistic element (speech sounds or letters). Performance on the visuospatial working memory task was correlated with rapid digit naming. Among children with dyslexia, there was a significant main effect of a KIAA0319 variant previously associated with neural inconsistency on reaction times in the rapid speech task and a nominally significant effect on RAN performance. Overall, we provide evidence for general processing speed deficits in dyslexia, though more research is needed to determine the relationship to candidate-dyslexia genes.

articles.title: Problem gambling and physical blind box and card pack and digital loot box spending: a Mainland Chinese survey
articles.authors: Leon Y. Xiao; Loïs Fournier; Charlotte Eben
articles.abstract: Gambling-like products share structural and psychological characteristics with legally regulated traditional gambling but are generally not regulated as gambling. Virtual gambling-like products include video game loot boxes, whilst physical gambling-like products include blind boxes and card packs. Stakeholders are concerned about the potential harms of these globally popular products, including overspending and the normalization of gambling amongst children. We surveyed Mainland Chinese video game players (final N = 913) to investigate whether spending on various gambling-like products is associated with problem gambling severity. Replicating previous results, we found weak—but practically meaningful—associations between problem gambling severity and both digital loot box and physical card pack spending. In contrast, the association between problem gambling and physical blind box spending was very weak and arguably not practically meaningful. Fundamental differences at the product characteristic-level mean that some gambling-like products, like blind boxes, may be less risky, but further research is warranted. Thus, a cautious and balanced approach with a focus on product transparency and child protection should be taken when regulating gambling-like products. Blind box regulation may justifiably be light-touch, whilst loot box and card pack regulations could be stricter and more restrictive, given a greater potential for harm. Preregistered Stage 1 protocol: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/PYFQV (date of in-principle acceptance: 18 March 2026).

articles.title: From the app to the lexicon: Neurocognitive markers of word integration in a second language
articles.authors: Ramón Igarreta; Luz Bavassi; Laura Kaczer
articles.abstract: The consolidation of newly learned vocabulary into semantic memory networks is a critical process in word learning, including second-language (L2) acquisition. However, most neurocognitive studies of lexical-semantic integration rely on short, artificial learning paradigms, leaving open the question of whether naturalistic, app-based learning produces comparable neural outcomes. In this study, we combined an ecological learning environment with controlled electrophysiological testing to examine whether vocabulary learned through Duolingo shows neural signatures of semantic integration. Native Spanish speakers studied Guarani vocabulary for five weeks and subsequently completed a semantic decision task during EEG recording that included both L1 (Spanish) and L2 (Guarani) word pairs. Critically, L2 targets were classified as remote (learned earlier during the five-week training and not practiced in the final stage) or recent (learned in the final training stage and tested approximately 10 days later), allowing us to assess consolidation-related differences. Behaviorally, participants responded more accurately and faster to L1 than L2 words, and accuracy for related items was higher for remotely than recently learned items, consistent with consolidation-related strengthening. Electrophysiologically, robust N400 priming effects emerged for remotely learned words—whereas no facilitation was observed for recent words. This graded pattern suggests that only words with extended consolidation time exhibited neural markers of lexical–semantic integration. Together, these findings demonstrate that combining real-world digital learning with controlled neural testing can reveal how naturalistic language experience shapes the neurocognitive dynamics of word learning and consolidation.

articles.title: Do people who care about their data and privacy know their data rights? Evidence from Estonia, 2023–2025
articles.authors: Tanel Mällo; Jaan Tulviste
articles.abstract:
European data protection law gives people rights over their personal data, but what mo-
tivates us to exercise those rights? In three surveys of Estonian adults (2023–2025), we
examined whether people who care about privacy also know their data protection rights.
Respondents valued privacy far more than they felt they had it and regarded all seven
types of personal data asked about as sensitive; valuing privacy, attention to privacy, ex-
perienced privacy and security, and perceived data sensitivity rose slightly over the period.
Knowledge of data rights, by contrast, was low, did not rise, and was unrelated to privacy
and data sensitivity. The same five combinations of sensitivity and knowledge recurred
in all three waves, and sociodemographic characteristics explained little of them. Caring
about personal data and privacy were thus unrelated to knowing one’s rights, so efforts
should be made to explain and bridge the gap between privacy/data concerns and the
individual opportunities to mitigate them.

articles.title: From Echo Chambers to Echo Machines? Endorsement, Evidence, and the Certainty of Belief in Conversations With AI
articles.authors: Olivier LE BON; Xavier Noël
articles.abstract: Randomized trials show that conversations with large language models (LLMs) can reduce conspiracy belief and, more modestly, political polarization. Yet the same systems can increase conspiracy belief when instructed to, and clinical reports describe chatbot conversations accompanying the escalation of implausible convictions. Prevailing accounts attribute both outcomes to the evidence a model supplies. We note that most experiments confound evidence about the world with endorsement of the person, and that the clearest attempt to separate them favors evidence. Drawing on research on attitude certainty, self-validation, and responses to flattery, we distinguish the position of a belief from the certainty with which it is held and formalize γ, an effect of endorsement on certainty at fixed factual content, interpretable as a validation gain. If higher certainty lowers responsiveness to later evidence, the account permits a conditional outcome: beliefs that become less extreme yet more rigid, without any misinformation. We specify two critical experiments, a factorial test of facts and endorsement that includes a source known to approve everyone and an endorsement-first design with counterevidence held constant, plus an articulation control. Conversational AI becomes a test bench for an old question: can social approval make subsequent evidence matter less?

articles.title: Can GenAI Boost Writing Scores? Another Robust Bayesian Meta-Analysis (RoBMA) of Writing Ability
articles.authors: Shawn Hemelstrand
articles.abstract: A new meta-analysis (Teng, 2026) has shown that genAI has a strong impact on writing with similar effects as another recent meta-analysis (Dong, 2026). The current analysis instead shows a much weaker effect after correcting for entry errors and heterogeneity.

articles.title: Designing AI-Agents with Personalities: A Psychometric Approach
articles.authors: Muhua Huang; Xijuan Zhang; Christopher J. Soto; James Evans
articles.abstract: We introduce a methodology for assigning quantifiable and psychometrically validated personalities to AI-Agents using the Big Five framework. Across three studies, we evaluate its feasibility and limitations. In Study 1, we show that large language models (LLMs) capture semantic similarities among Big Five measures, providing a basis for personality assignment. In Study 2, we create AI-Agents using prompts designed based on the Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2) in different format, and find that AI-Agents powered by new models align more closely with human responses on the Mini-Markers test, although the finer pattern of results (e.g., factor loading patterns) were sometimes inconsistent. In Study 3, we validate our AI-Agents on risk-taking and moral dilemma vignettes, finding that models prompted with the BFI-2-Expanded format most closely reproduce human personality-decision associations, while safety-aligned models generally inflate ‘moral’ ratings. Overall, our results show that AI-Agents align with humans in correlations between input Big Five traits and output responses and may serve as useful tools for preliminary research. Nevertheless, discrepancies in finer response patterns indicate that AI-Agents cannot (yet) fully substitute for human participants in precision or high-stakes projects.

articles.title: Examining Individual Differences in Misinformation Engagement among Social Media Users in a Simulated Twitter Task
articles.authors: Dyuthi Dinesh; Michael Robert Haupt
articles.abstract:
Background 
Psychological traits and social identities have been linked to misinformation sharing, but most studies measure passive or low-effort engagement. Less is known about high-effort engagement that requires users to write a response. We examined whether cognitive reflection, motivated reasoning variables (political orientation, religiosity, trust in medical scientists) and personality traits are differentially associated with liking, retweeting, replying to, and quoting COVID-19 misinformation and public-health-unaligned tweets.
Methods 
US MTurk participants (N = 858; September 2021) engaged with real COVID-19 tweets in a simulated Twitter feed. Replies and quotes were manually coded as endorsive or combative. We fit OLS regressions for each engagement type (N = 851) and estimated relative importance using Shapley (LMG) decomposition of R².
Results
Endorsive replies and quotes were rare (7.3% and 4.3% of participants for misinformation). Political conservatism and religiosity were associated with endorsive misinformation replies, and motivated reasoning variables were the largest contributors in all reply and quote models, though these models explained little variance (adjusted R² ≤ .03). Cognitive reflection was negatively associated only with liking, and grandiose narcissism was the largest contributor to retweeting.
Conclusion
Classical reasoning, personality and motivated reasoning explanations of misinformation propagation were each supported, depending on the type of engagement. Simulation tasks that measure multiple engagement behaviors can help clarify inconsistent findings in the misinformation literature.

articles.title: From Bulking to Cutting: Social Media, Self-Esteem, and Disordered Eating in Young Men
articles.authors: Jakub Smolinski; Jaynie Rance; Menna Price
articles.abstract: Bulking and cutting (caloric surplus and restriction) are increasingly common among young men but remain under-researched within disordered eating frameworks. This study examined social media use and self-esteem as predictors, as well as their association with disordered eating and bulking and cutting behaviours. Seventy-six physically active UK men aged 18-25 years (M = 22.07, SD = 2.07) completed online measures of social media use, self-esteem, disordered eating (restraint, eating concern, shape concern, weight concern), and bulking and cutting behaviours. Higher social media use predicted higher eating concern (p = .003), while lower self-esteem predicted higher eating and shape concerns (p = .029, p = <.001). Neither social media use nor self-esteem predicted restraint, bulking, or cutting. Exploratory mediation analyses showed that restraint fully mediated the association between shape concern and cutting behaviour (p = < .001). Social media use and self-esteem appear to relate to specific disordered eating symptoms, whereas bulking and cutting may be more closely linked to restraint processes. These findings support expanding conceptualisations of disordered eating in young men to include muscle-oriented dietary behaviours and their distinct psychological pathways.

articles.title: Multiple Methods for Visualizing Human Language: A Tutorial for Social and Behavioural Scientists
articles.authors: Veerle Celine Eijsbroek; August Nilsson; Leon Ackermann; Zhuojun Gu; Clara Wiebel; Adithya V Ganesan; Katarina Kjell; H. Andrew Schwartz; Oscar Nils Erik Kjell
articles.abstract:
Humans use language to communicate psychological experiences. Advancements in Natural Language
Processing have enabled researchers to quantitatively study and assess psychological states and
behaviors through language (e.g., well-being and mental health). Insights from language analyses are
often best conveyed through visualizations. Data-driven visualizations of how language statistically
relates to psychological dimensions can help interpret assessment scores, uncover meaningful patterns,
and understand the intricate relationships between language use and mental states. Visualizations can
be used to differentiate between related constructs (e.g., How does language related to depression versus
anxiety differ?), understand the validity of assessment tools (e.g., Does the language related to high
depression severity match with depression theory?), and explain language-based assessments (e.g.,
Which language is indicative of higher depression severity in a language-based assessment?).

This tutorial demonstrates how to transform language data into visual insights using the text and topics
packages in R. We provide practical guidance on creating four types of visualizations based on different
language analysis techniques, examining how language use patterns are statistically associated with a
psychological construct. We visualize 1) individual words and phrases (n-grams), 2) topics (word
clusters), 3) words in the word embedding space, and 4) relevant language examples. These different
visualizations offer complementary perspectives, visualizing linguistic elements from individual words
to overarching topics and text examples. The underlying methods range from correlations between
individual words to more advanced techniques, including topic modeling and Large Language Models.
By making these methods accessible, this tutorial aims to empower researchers to use language
visualizations for meaningful, data-driven insights.

articles.title: Not passive sponges: When attention wanes, our brains are less synchronized with the environment
articles.authors: Elena Greatti; Laura Batterink; Davide Crepaldi; Amy Finn
articles.abstract: Without even being aware, humans are amazingly sensitive to the structures around them. Is this sensitivity constant or does it fluctuate along with our attentional states? To answer this foundational question, we deployed temporally sensitive measures that allow us to track neural entrainment—the synchronization of brain activity to environmental regularities—alongside fluctuations in attentional states. Participants (n = 78) viewed both random and structured visual streams while performing a task to index fluctuating attentional states. Structured streams evoked robust neural entrainment and reduced attentional lapses. Moreover, attentional states varied with neural entrainment. Across participants, those who displayed greater neural entrainment had reduced attentional lapses. And critically, even within individuals, greater entrainment was observed during periods of greater attentional focus. Our sensitivity to structure and attentional states are therefore inextricably linked: structures stabilize our attentional states and our sensitivity to structure dynamically mirrors the ebb and flow of human attention.

articles.title: Machines in the Middle: How AI Use Changes What Coworkers Think of, and Do for, One Another
articles.authors: Maxine Parker; Celine Huang; Sekoul Krastev
articles.abstract: Generative AI is now embedded in how coworkers, leaders, and organizations communicate, yet its effects on the relationships among them are still poorly understood. This review synthesizes recent research on how an individual’s AI use changes the way others perceive, judge, and behave toward them, and shows that these effects can be explained by established theories of human-human interaction, including attribution theory, computers-as-social-actors, the integrative model of organizational trust, social exchange theory, and resource-based theories. The evidence suggests that observers often read AI use as a sign of disposition rather than circumstance, judging AI users as less competent, motivated, warm, and authentic, and that disclosure does not repair the resulting loss of trust. These perceptions carry over into behavior: coworkers reciprocate less, share less knowledge, and show less prosocial behavior toward AI users, while AI-related job insecurity, loneliness, and work alienation further strain ties among colleagues. AI use also loosens moral standards and shifts how blame is assigned, making people more critical of others’ work but more lenient toward misconduct. These effects are conditional rather than uniformly negative. AI can reduce loneliness, improve coordination, and prompt employees to invest more in emotionally supportive ties, and relational buffers such as leader-member exchange, shared leadership, and supervisor support can offset its costs. The review concludes that AI’s costs to workplace relationships run mainly through indirect pathways, not through the technology itself. It outlines organizational implications, including clear norms for when and why AI is used and protection of socially valued tasks, and identifies priorities for future research: longitudinal designs, team- and network-level studies, intervention research, and more diverse samples.

articles.title: Do Sexual Beliefs Shape Relationship Quality Over Time? Evidence From Early Romantic Relationships
articles.authors: Jessica Caferri; Akshita Uppot; Stephanie Raposo; Emily Impett; Amy Muise; SHaRe Lab
articles.abstract: Satisfying romantic relationships are important for well-being yet are difficult to maintain, as sexual satisfaction and relationship quality often decline across early relationship development. Sexual growth and destiny beliefs reflect whether sexual satisfaction is viewed as something that develops through effort or depends on natural, inherent compatibility. Such beliefs may be associated with how couples navigate changes in their relationship. Using longitudinal data from 161 couples (N= 322) early in their relationship, followed over 18 months, we examined whether individuals’ and their partners’ sexual beliefs predicted trajectories of sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and commitment. Relationship satisfaction and commitment showed small declines over time, whereas sexual satisfaction and sexual beliefs remained relatively stable. Higher actor and partner sexual growth beliefs were associated with higher levels of all outcomes in general, and individuals with partners’ higher in sexual growth beliefs were buffered from steeper declines in relationship satisfaction and commitment over time. In contrast, higher actor, but not partner, sexual destiny beliefs were associated with lower relationship satisfaction and commitment in general. Overall, the findings suggest that sexual beliefs function as relatively stable cognitive frameworks, with partner sexual growth beliefs playing a role in protecting relationship quality and commitment during early relationship development.

articles.title: Minds Meet Machines: The Joint Role of Trust and Intellectual Humility in AI Persuasion
articles.authors: Devora Newman; Almog Simchon; Ruth Mayo
articles.abstract: Research shows that AI models have a remarkable ability to change people’s minds following a short conversation, a notoriously difficult task for human communicators. Such persuasive paradigms provide a unique opportunity to examine which psychological characteristics predict receptivity to counter-attitudinal information. We focus on two characteristics: intellectual humility (IH), reflecting openness to revising one’s beliefs following new information, and trust in the information source (AI). To establish the role of a-priori dispositions that determine acceptance of new information, we ran two online studies, sampling British participants with a negative attitude toward legal immigrants (N = 294). We replicated previous findings showing significant and lasting attitude change following a brief exchange with GPT, but crucially, this effect was not uniform. In Study 1, attitude change was greatest among participants with higher initial trust in AIs and higher intellectual humility. Study 2 extended this finding by measuring both dispositions a week before the conversation with GPT, revealing the same pattern: opinion change was greatest among those who were both open to new information and trusting of its source. These findings highlight the centrality of recipient dispositions, suggesting that the relationship between source trust and persuasion depends on recipients' intellectual humility. More broadly, source trust may function as more than a heuristic cue, and its relationship with attitude change may depend on recipients' willingness to recognize the fallibility of their beliefs. Together, these findings extend perspectives on persuasion by highlighting the joint role of source trust and recipients' epistemic dispositions in belief revision.

articles.title: Facilitation by Irrelevant Distractors Under High Perceptual Load: Suppression or Controlled Distractor Prioritization?
articles.authors: Greta Manini; Francisco Garre-Frutos; Fabiano Botta; Elisa Martín-Arévalo; Juan Lupiáñez
articles.abstract: Perceptual load theory is a key framework in visual attention research, demonstrating that under high-load conditions, fully irrelevant distractors are no longer processed and do not disrupt task performance. In our recent work (Manini et al., 2026), we replicated this effect. However, we also found that under high load, the distractor not only failed to impair performance but actually led to faster reaction times (RTs) in distractor-present trials. In the attentional capture literature, this reversed effect is typically considered to reflect distractor suppression. However, in the perceptual load task, where the distractor is placed outside the relevant search array, suppression should not logically lead to faster responses. Furthermore, the faster responses were accompanied by increased error rates, leading us to hypothesize that this reversed effect may reflect some form of distractor prioritization rather than distractor suppression. To test this hypothesis, we first analyzed the consistency of this effect across all available open-data resources using the Forster and Lavie (2008b) task. We then reanalyzed the same data, incorporating the spatial proximity between target and distractor as an additional variable: distractors appearing near the target strongly drove the reversed RT effect, while distractors presented far from the target led to increased error rates. These findings challenge the idea that high perceptual load prevents the processing of irrelevant stimuli. Moreover, they suggest that faster RTs in distractor-present conditions do not necessarily indicate distractor suppression, as commonly assumed in attentional capture research, offering new insight into the interpretation of behavioral observations in this field.

articles.title: Celebrity Endorsement and Meditation Intention: A Randomized Experiment
articles.authors: Michael Bowen
articles.abstract: Meditation offers well-documented health benefits, yet persistence with meditation is low. Drawing on the Reasoned Action Approach, we tested whether celebrity meditators as a descriptive-norm cue improve attitudes toward and intention to meditate. In this randomized survey experiment (N = 2,035), participants viewed one of four images captioned "Meditating for just a few minutes a day can transform your mind". Compared to same-gender non-celebrities, the celebrity images did not increase intention to meditate (female: OR = 0.88, 95% CI 0.64–1.21; male: OR = 1.18, 0.85–1.63) or change attitudes (female: b = −0.09, −0.19 to 0.00; male: b = 0.06, −0.03 to 0.14; all Holm-adjusted p ≥ .24). In conclusion, a single exposure to a celebrity meditator may be insufficient to shift attitudes or intentions toward meditation.

articles.title: Gamblers' behavior in a self-exclusion system with social barriers to revocation: evidence from Chile
articles.authors: Omar D. Perez; José Rafael Arenas Rojas; Mario Sanclemente Villegas; Steve Sharman
articles.abstract:
Background and aims: In most self-exclusion programs, leaving is the gambler's own decision. In Chile, by contrast, revocation requires the consent of a sponsor whom the participant nominates at enrollment and may later replace. We investigated whether the relationship with the first sponsor, and later changes of sponsor, relate to how long participants remain excluded.

Methods: We analyzed records from Chile's self-exclusion registry (2019–2025; N = 3,825 participants; 1,753 revocations). Time to first revocation was examined using Kaplan–Meier curves and time-varying Cox models including the relationship with the first sponsor, the direction of replacements, and prior rejected requests, accounting for the three-month waiting period after a replacement.

Results: Participants whose first sponsor was a close family member had a lower revocation hazard than those who nominated a partner (HR = 0.67, 95% CI 0.59–0.76); their median time to revocation was 40.4 months, against 20 to 22 months in the other groups. More importantly, replacing a non-family sponsor with a close family member was followed by a lower hazard (HR = 0.59), whereas the reverse change showed no detectable difference. Each rejected request, and each replacement once the waiting period had ended, was associated with a higher hazard, with many revocations right after that period.

Discussion and conclusions: Having a close family member as sponsor, whether from enrollment or after a replacement, is associated with longer exclusions. These results are discussed in the light of the sponsor's role as a social commitment device and the points at which participants may benefit from support.

articles.title: Data Transparency in Industrial, Work, and Organizational Psychology: A Primer on Data Sharing and Documentation of Data Reuse
articles.authors: Maie Stein; Richard Janzen; Cort W. Rudolph; Hannes Zacher
articles.abstract: Data transparency is fundamental for evaluating the validity of empirical findings, supporting cumulative knowledge building, and strengthening the credibility of science in society. However, data sharing (i.e., making research data available to others) and transparent documentation of data reuse (i.e., reporting the use of the same data across multiple publications) are not yet standard practice in industrial, work, and organizational (IWO) psychology. The aim of this primer is to discuss the important role of these data transparency practices in advancing open science and to provide practical guidance for the adoption of these practices in IWO psychology. We review the benefits and challenges of data sharing and outline recommendations for researchers, reviewers, and journal editors in IWO psychology to support its implementation. We also examine the implications of data reuse for the interpretation and accumulation of empirical evidence and propose several approaches for transparently documenting data reuse.

articles.title: Displayed judgment certainty reorganizes source selection in self-formed networks
articles.authors: Gaël Carniel; Valentin Guigon; Frédéric Moisan; Alain Barrat; Jean-Claude Dreher
articles.abstract: Collective intelligence in self-formed networks depends on which judgments people choose to observe, as well as on how they integrate those judgments. We tested whether displaying judgment certainty reorganizes source selection and improves subsequent accuracy. Across eight online sessions, 273 participants evaluated 14 true and false news headlines, formed costly directed observation networks, and revised their beliefs over five updates. During network formation, we manipulated the visibility of certainty, defined by the extremity of each source's private probability judgment, while belief direction and source accuracy remained hidden. Displaying certainty produced denser networks and redirected links toward more certain sources; current popularity also predicted selection. Visibility increased exposure to highly certain but incorrect judgments, without a clear improvement in the relative accuracy of selected sources. Accuracy increased across repeated judgments, but certainty visibility did not detectably increase this improvement and reduced reconstructed net scores under the task's payoff structure. Observations with selected sources showed greater improvement than those without, and improvement was associated with selected sources' initial accuracy. Belief revisions moved toward selected sources and decreased with participants' own certainty. Among six compact predictive models, certainty-reinforcing DeGroot provided the best penalized and aggregate held-out prediction, although it did not capture the large first update. These findings distinguish a cue's ability to attract attention from its ability to identify useful information: displayed certainty can reorganize costly information acquisition without a detectable average accuracy benefit.

articles.title: Altered pre-supplementary motor area recruitment during semantic inhibition in individuals with elevated obsessive–compulsive traits
articles.authors: Rebeca Villarroel; Francisco Marcano; José Luis González-Mora; Manuel de Vega; Iván Padrón González; Mariano Díaz-Rivera; Damián Jan; Cristián Modroño
articles.abstract:
Background: Inhibitory control dysfunction has been implicated in obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD), but neuroimaging research has focused predominantly on motor response inhibition. Whether obsessive–compulsive traits are associated with altered neural recruitment during semantic inhibition remains unclear.
Methods: Forty right-handed participants with lower or elevated obsessive–compulsive traits performed an fMRI adaptation of the Hayling Sentence Completion Task. Participants either selected an expected sentence completion (initiation) or suppressed this strongly prepotent response to select an unrelated word (inhibition). Whole-brain and anatomically defined region-of-interest (ROI) analyses examined task-related activation and Group × Condition interactions, with particular interest in the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA) and SMA proper.
Results: Semantic inhibition produced a robust behavioural cost in reaction times and error rates, with no significant differences between groups. Whole-brain analysis identified the strongest inhibition-related activation in the left preSMA. The exploratory Group × Condition analysis also yielded its peak interaction in this region. Anatomically defined ROI analysis showed a significant Group × Condition interaction in the preSMA after family-wise error correction (t = 2.56, pFWE = .012), reflecting a larger inhibition-related increase in controls compared to individuals with elevated obsessive–compulsive traits. The corresponding interaction in SMA proper did not reach statistical significance (t = 1.74, pFWE = .084).
Conclusions: Elevated obsessive–compulsive traits were associated with altered preSMA recruitment during semantic inhibition in absence of behavioural impairment. This extends neural markers of obsessive–compulsive alterations from the domain of motor inhibition to that of semantic inhibition.

articles.title: Neuroscience-informed psychoeducation for cognitive rehabilitation
articles.authors: Jamie Berry; Marc L. Copersino
articles.abstract:
This chapter describes a neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) approach to
cognitive rehabilitation (CR) following acquired brain injury (ABI), with primary
emphasis on traumatic brain injury and stroke. NIPE is conceptualised as more than
information provision: neuroscience-informed explanations are used to help patients
and families understand cognitive difficulties, recovery, rehabilitation strategies, and
their implications for everyday functioning. Neuropsychological feedback is presented
as a common context for NIPE, with attention to tailoring, functional translation,
multimodal support, and verification of understanding.
A dual-lens framework is proposed for NIPE delivery in CR. The therapeutic lens
emphasises alliance, empathy and warmth, person-centred collaboration, shared
explanatory models, and goal setting. The cognition-informed lens addresses how
cognitive difficulties may affect learning through adjustment of information load and
pacing, repetition, clear and concrete language, integration with existing knowledge,
teach-back, and multimodal delivery. Together, these lenses inform considerations of
timing and context and seven structural principles of NIPE: trustworthiness, interaction,
salience, motivation, intensity, repetition, and multimodal/multimedia delivery.
The chapter also considers NIPE content related to neuroplasticity, prognosis and
recovery, rehabilitation approaches, and factors that may influence functioning and
participation. Throughout, emphasis is placed on distinguishing established evidence
from plausible but untested mechanisms and on presenting recovery in probabilistic
rather than deterministic terms.

articles.title: Are Workplace Tolerance and Individual Autonomy associated with Work Engagement? —Mediation analyses with Psychological Safety and Intrinsic Motivation
articles.authors: Takazumi Ono; Ryota Shin; Aoba Tamura; Yukihiko Okada; Hiroko Costantini; Misato Nihei
articles.abstract: There is growing recognition of the importance of designing work environments that promote the well-being of diverse employees. Although the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model has contributed substantially to work engagement research, there remains scope to extend it to address the challenge of creating inclusive work environments. We examined the associations of workplace tolerance and individual autonomy with work engagement, including the potential mediating roles of psychological safety and intrinsic motivation. We used data from 1084 Japanese workers collected across four waves of online surveys and conducted causal mediation analyses. As a result, the presence of tolerant coworkers was associated with work engagement through workplace psychological safety (total effect = 0.296; proportion mediated = 29.7 %), whereas the absence of intolerant coworkers was not clearly associated with work engagement. Individual autonomy was also associated with work engagement through intrinsic motivation (total effect = 0.444), although the proportion mediated was modest (14.5 %). These findings suggest that positioning workplace tolerance and individual autonomy as social and personal resources, respectively, may extend the JD–R model by enabling it to describe the conditions under which employees with diverse characteristics and circumstances can engage in their work on an equitable basis.

articles.title: Linguistic Markers of Self-Representation Reflect Daily Emotional Experiences in an Expressive Writing Study
articles.authors: Emily Huang; Claire Whiting; Steven Mesquiti; Sofia S. Baran; Erik C Nook
articles.abstract: The words people use provide important insights into their emotional experiences. Several measures for tracking emotions through language have been developed, including sentiment (i.e., the positivity and negativity of language) and I-usage (first-person singular pronoun use, thought to reflect negative self-focus). However, emerging research using large language model embedding techniques has quantified not just if people use “I” but how they use it, yielding a measure of self-representation (i.e., how strongly people see themselves as “good” and “able” rather than “bad” and “unable”). This measure tracks mental health outcomes in psychotherapy. Given that emotions and emotion regulation are intimately connected to how we view ourselves, linguistic self-representations may also offer a means for assessing emotional experiences. Here, we examined the associations between participants’ linguistic self-representations and daily emotional experiences in a 14-day expressive writing study (N = 53). Within-person associations showed that on days when participants’ self-representation embedding scores were closer to “good” or “able,” they reported more positive and less negative emotions. At the between-person level, people with self-representations overall closer to “good” experienced lower negative emotional reactivity to expressive writing. These findings suggest that linguistic markers of self-representation hold promise as a tool for assessing emotional experiences, extending prior work linking it to mental health. Translations of these findings could contribute to earlier identification of changes in emotional functioning and provide new ways of assessing metrics of mental health through everyday language.

articles.title: Noradrenaline-centric bias in the pupil-linked arousal literature
articles.authors: Simon van Gaal; Lola Beerendonk; Haoyue Zhang; Tobias H. Donner; Jan Willem de Gee
articles.abstract: The literature on pupil-linked arousal shows a pervasive bias: it often attributes findings to the noradrenergic locus coeruleus while overlooking other neuromodulatory systems. Here, we quantify the extent of this bias and emphasize that correcting it is essential for refining theoretical models and improving interpretability in this rapidly evolving field.

articles.title: Connected or drained? An experience sampling study on informal communication and well-being in hybrid work settings
articles.authors: Alicia Andrea Meier-Ernst; Leonard Reinecke
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Informal communication has been ascribed well-being functions. Yet in increasingly hybrid work settings, where employees work remotely, informal exchanges frequently occur via digital channels and may hinder relational bonds and drain rather than restore employees’ energy. Drawing on Communicate Bond Belong Theory, this study examines whether informal communication enhances or undermines employees’ well-being in hybrid settings by considering its perceived quality, relational benefits, and energy-related costs. Design/methodology/approach: A one-week experience sampling study (26 participants; 549 surveys) captured employees’ everyday communication episodes with co-workers and their subsequent experiences. Mixed-effects models estimated within-person relationships while accounting for between-person differences.
Findings: Episodes that were more informal than usual were associated with higher striving potential (e.g., more pleasantness or meaningfulness). In turn, higher striving potential was associated with more relatedness need satisfaction and a more favorable relatedness-to-energy ratio, though not with energy expenditure. Communication modality did not moderate these associations. However, text-based (vs. audio-visual) exchanges were significantly associated with lower relatedness and energy expenditure, and a higher relatedness-to-energy ratio. Originality: Adopting a situational perspective, this study moves beyond frequency-based and between-person approaches to everyday informal communication. It disentangles message- and channel-related effects and their distinct contributions in the relationship between informal talk and employee well-being. From this novel perspective, the findings provide evidence that informal communication is a resource for employees’ well-being, but can impose demands when it occurs digitally, an aspect that practitioners should recognize when designing informal communication initiatives.

articles.title: How to end a nightmare using ocular distress signaling
articles.authors: Remington Mallett; Norah Wolk; Daniel Morris; Yasmeen Nahas; Cameron Sandell; Karen Konkoly; Michelle Carr; Ken A. Paller
articles.abstract: Nightmares trap people in a unique state of helplessness. Whereas fear during wake can be resolved with downregulation strategies, fear during sleep typically coincides with a reduction in the cognitive and social routes to implement them. Here, we report a case in which a dreamer and a technician together overcame both limitations, ending a nightmare in real time. A participant experiencing frequent nightmares was enrolled in a protocol designed to induce lucid dreams (restoring cognition during REM sleep) and enable communication from the dream via eye movements (restoring a social connection). During a nightmare, they gained awareness and used the eye signal as a mayday to request extraction from the dream, all while in polysomnography-verified REM sleep. They were awakened by the technician 34 seconds after the help request and reported immediate relief. At 2- and 4-week follow-ups, lucid dream frequency increased relative to baseline, with lucidity reducing the distress of a subsequent nightmare. Together, these results suggest that real-time dream communication might offer an in somno approach to treating nightmares, a core symptom of PTSD and other psychiatric disorders.

articles.title: Trusting the Machine: Separating Trust in GenAI Authors from Trust in Their Content
articles.authors: Caroline Simpson; Clara Colombatto; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang
articles.abstract: As Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) becomes more sophisticated and widespread, it matters how its perceived humanness affects trust. Previous work shows that anthropomorphism increases an agent’s perceived trustworthiness as an advisor. We asked whether an author’s presentation also affects trust in the information it produces in a non-advisory role. In two experiments, participants read a science communication blog post attributed to an author with varying anthropomorphic cues. They rated the trustworthiness of the author (author trust) and the content (content trust). In Experiment 1 (N = 270), the post was attributed to a GenAI author described with low or high anthropomorphic cues, or to a human expert. The human author, who also differed in implied professional expertise, received higher author trust than either GenAI author. This effect was reliably larger than the effect on content trust. The low- and high-cue GenAI authors did not reliably differ, including in anthropomorphism ratings. In Experiment 2 (N = 148, preregistered), participants chatted with a GenAI chatbot, presented as the author, that used fewer (low condition) or more (high condition) anthropomorphic cues. The high-cue chatbot was rated more anthropomorphic and received modestly higher author trust. No reliable content trust effect was detected, and evidence that the two effects differed was inconclusive. Author and content trust were strongly correlated in both experiments. These results suggest that cues to an author’s humanness may shape trust in the author more than in what it communicates, although the clearest evidence came from comparing human and GenAI authors.

articles.title: Seeing a partner’s gestures in conversation increases referential but not form alignment: Evidence for distinct mechanisms of alignment in co-speech gestures
articles.authors: Sho Akamine; antje meyer; Asli Ozyurek
articles.abstract: People often align with one another’s sentence structures, lexical choices, and co-speech gestures during conversation. Such linguistic alignment has been attributed to both low-level priming and high-level collaborative efforts to establish mutual understanding (grounding). Although the contributions of these processes have been extensively investigated for verbal aspects of language use, their roles in co-speech gestural alignment remain largely unexplored. Here, we manipulated partner visibility in a video-mediated dyadic referential communication game (n = 45 dyads) to examine (i) whether priming and grounding contribute to the two dimensions of gestural alignment: referential and form alignment, and (ii) how lexical alignment relates to gestural alignment. We found that participants produced referentially aligned gestures more frequently when they could see their partner’s gestures than when they could not, irrespective of whether their own gestures were visible to their partner. This pattern provides evidence consistent with priming, but not with the predicted grounding effect. By contrast, visibility had little to no effect on Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)-based gesture form similarity, suggesting that the contributions of priming and grounding may differ between referential and form alignment. Furthermore, lexical alignment was positively associated with the frequency of referentially aligned gestures, even after accounting for control variables. This association is consistent with the possibility that shared conceptualization of referents contributes to gestural alignment. Taken together, these findings highlight that mechanisms underlying alignment may differ depending on the dimensions of gestural alignment and point to distinct roles for priming and shared conceptualization in the alignment of co-speech gestures.

articles.title: Developing human-AI complementarity: Augmenting everyday decision making with Large Language Models
articles.authors: Adrian Paul Banks; David M Gamblin
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can improve human judgement, but human–AI systems rarely achieve complementarity: combined performance exceeding that of both humans and AI alone. Across three longitudinal studies (N = 671), we tested whether large language models (LLMs) could support complementarity by contributing to the construction and revision of everyday decision representations. Participants reported real, personally meaningful decisions involving two options and the decision outcome success one week later. As decisions were participant-generated rather than predefined, LLMs dynamically generated considerations and alternative evaluations tailored to each decision. We compared the predictive validity of AI, Human, and augmented evaluations. AI evaluations were standalone LLM predictions of decision outcome success. Human weighted-additive evaluations combined participant-generated attributes, importance weights, and option ratings. Augmented evaluations incorporated LLM-generated attributes and, in later studies, suggested weights and ratings, while participants selected attributes and retained control over evaluations. Augmented evaluations consistently predicted experienced outcomes and showed the strongest observed associations across all three studies. Evidence for complementarity was clearest in Study 2, where fully augmented evaluations outperformed both standalone approaches and explained additional variance in expected and experienced outcomes beyond the standalone evaluations considered together. Across studies, augmentation expanded the attribute set, with participants retaining human and AI contributions. These findings show that human–AI complementarity can emerge in predicting success of real decision outcomes and suggest that decision architecture matters. A distributed cognitive system that integrates AI contributions across all stages of decision making while humans remain responsible for selection and judgement of personally relevant considerations offers a promising architecture for evaluating diverse, personally meaningful real-life decisions.

articles.title: iOS Shortcuts as a Free, No-Code Tool for Event-Triggered Experience Sampling
articles.authors: Douglas A. Parry; Tilo Hartmann
articles.abstract: Event-triggered experience sampling prompts in situ surveys when specific behaviors or contexts occur. This approach is valuable for capturing infrequent or context-bound experiences but often requires custom or expensive software. This article describes how iOS Shortcuts, a pre-installed automation feature, can provide a free, no-code alternative for event-triggered surveys on iPhones. Using trigger-action programming, researchers can configure automations that launch survey URLs with embedded contextual parameters when designated events occur. We describe the procedure, outline a workflow of triggers, actions, and embedded variables, and illustrate the approach with worked examples and templates.

articles.title: What Drives Leaders to Serve? The Joint and Interactive Effects of HEXACO Personality Traits and Implicit Motives on Servant Leadership
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: Drawing on the channeling hypothesis (Winter et al., 1998), this study examines the role of leaders’ explicit personality traits, implicit motives, and their interaction in predicting servant leadership. Using a dyadic design (N = 219), supervisors completed measures of their HEXACO personality traits and implicit motives, while subordinates rated their servant leadership behavior. Contrary to expectations, neither personality traits nor implicit motives explained unique variance in servant leadership. However, interactions between explicit traits and implicit motives significantly improved prediction. Specifically, leaders high in affiliation motivation were perceived as more servant when they scored high on extraversion and, contrary to expectations, low on agreeableness. These findings highlight the value of considering both implicit motives and explicit traits, as well as their interplay, in understanding servant leadership.

articles_hidden.title: Putting social, emotional, and behavioral skills to work: SEB skills are robustly linked with occupational attainment, attitudes, behaviors, interests, and values
articles_hidden.authors: Christopher J. Soto; Alexandra Glotzbach; Christopher Napolitano; Madison Nicole Sewell; Heejun Roy Yoon; Alex Casillas; Bo Zhang; Brent Roberts
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality traits are long-established correlates of occupational success. Recently, researchers have also begun to examine the role of social, emotional, and behavioral (SEB) skills in key life domains. Conceptualized as functional capacities rather than characteristic tendencies, SEB skills represent what individuals are capable of doing when wanted or needed. The present research examined how the five major skill domains assessed by the Behavioral, Emotional, and Social Skills Inventory (BESSI) relate with consequential work criteria and outcomes. Specifically, using a demographically representative sample of 1,064 working adults, we tested preregistered links of SEB skills with work performance, attainment, attitudes, intentions, behaviors, interests, and values. SEB skills related robustly with these criteria and outcomes, with different skill domains showing distinctive relationships. For example, Self-Management Skills were linked with self-perceived performance; Social Engagement Skills with occupational attainment; Cooperation Skills with prosocial interests and values; Emotional Resilience Skills with positive work attitudes; and Innovation Skills with creative interests and values. Short forms of the BESSI retained considerable predictive power, making them highly suitable for applied contexts. These findings highlight the key role of functional capacities in occupational experiences and provide a foundation for integrating SEB skills into personnel selection, career coaching, and organizational research.

articles_hidden.title: A Crucial Source of Psychological Certainty in Human Cognition: The Certainty Signature of Central Form
articles_hidden.authors: Paul Haward
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans often exhibit more certainty than is justified. Drawing on recent work in Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, the present paper proposes and tests a novel hypothesis about one important source of psychological certainty. On Form Theory, concepts have a central form: a core structure within each concept that stores a subset of its information, gives that information default influence in cognition, and activates a distinctive set of strong form-generated beliefs. The present paper tests the proposal that psychological certainty is one such form-generated belief. In Experiment 1, participants judged which properties would be present in newly encountered instances of familiar concepts. While they generalized both form and non-form properties to new instances, they reported being certain only for form properties. In Experiment 2, participants showed the same pattern for newly learned concepts. As soon as a property had been encoded as part of a concept’s central form, participants were much more likely to report being certain of its presence in a new instance than when the same property had been introduced in a generic sentence, but not as part of the concept’s central form. These findings help reveal a deep connection between psychological certainty and the structure of human concepts. Further, they suggest that conceptual structure is one important source of psychological certainty and provide a framework for investigating whether strongly held beliefs documented in research on stereotyping, memory, clinical depression, and conflict may sometimes derive from how concepts have been structured.

articles_hidden.title: Memory Overlap Shapes General and Specific Memory Differently in Adolescents and Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Merron Woodbury; Sagana Vijayarajah; Margaret Schlichting
articles_hidden.abstract: Over time we accumulate many interrelated memories which we draw upon to remember both generalities and specifics of our experience. While both aspects of memory improve through childhood, their maturation into adolescence remains poorly understood. Here, we compared how 39 adolescents (12-13 years old) and 36 adults managed differing levels of relatedness (“overlap”) among learned associations to remember shared (general) and unique (specific) features. Across age groups, greater overlap boosted memory for shared features but hindered memory for specifics. However, adolescents showed a reduced benefit of overlap for shared feature memory, suggesting they generalized across related memories differently than adults. Adolescents were also slower than adults to recognize unique features of highly overlapping memories, consistent with prolonged refinement of specific memory. Our results reveal continued maturation of both general and specific memory into adolescence while demonstrating how the overlaps among our experiences shape what we remember.

articles_hidden.title: A Tutorial on Multilevel Generalized Structured Component Analysis Using GSCA Pro
articles_hidden.authors: Sunmee Kim; Gyeongcheol Cho; Silvia Martelo-Landroguez; Gabriel Cepeda-Carrión; José L. Roldán; Heungsun Hwang
articles_hidden.abstract: Hierarchically structured data are common in behavioral and social science research, yet ignoring nested structures can lead to misleading statistical inferences and obscure meaningful variation in measurement and structural relationships across groups. Multilevel generalized structured component analysis (GSCA) extends component-based structural equation modeling to hierarchical data by allowing measurement loadings and structural path coefficients to vary across higher-level units while retaining common component weights. This tutorial introduces two-level GSCA and demonstrates its practical implementation using GSCA Pro, free software with a graphical interface. Data from 5,014 customers across four corporate chains provide a worked example. We guide readers through model specification, estimation, fit assessment, and interpretation of average and group-specific measurement and structural parameters, highlighting between-group heterogeneity.

articles_hidden.title: Mathematical Relationships Between Brains and Consciousness
articles_hidden.authors: Alexander Maier
articles_hidden.abstract: A chief aim of the neuroscience of consciousness is to derive how states of conscious experience (i.e., qualia) are related to supporting brain states (e.g., patterns of neural activation within patterns of neural connectivity). This aim goes beyond identifying neuronal correlates of consciousness (NCC) on the one side, and beyond structural descriptions of conscious experience (e.g., qualia structure) on the other side. The ultimate goal is to link these two sides by mapping specific neuronal states or mechanisms to specific conscious experiences. Relating two or more phenomena in science often takes the form of mathematical mappings, such as equations (e.g., E = mc^2). This raises the possibility that there also are mathematical mappings that relate conscious states to brain states. Here we review empirical work on mapping neuronal spiking activity to conscious contents. We specifically contrast pioneering paradigms aimed at identifying “bridge loci”, in the form of NCC, with paradigms aimed at identifying “bridge laws”, such as relating psychometric to neurometric functions. We then examine how these paradigms are augmented by mapping structural descriptions of conscious experience to structural descriptions of neuronal activity.

articles_hidden.title: Virtual Reality in Grief and Related Distress: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Pelin Sila Gelmez; Ayala Licht-Handler; Clare Killikelly
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Virtual Reality (VR) might support grieving processes through therapeuFc
environments that encourage conFnuing bonds with deceased loved ones. In contrast, VR might
encourage avoidance of reality among bereaved individuals and interfere with their grieving
processes.
Objective: This systematic review of studies with mixed methodological designs (i.e.,
qualitative, quantitative, mixed methods) examines the acceptability, feasibility and efficacy of
Virtual Reality (VR) for bereaved individuals.
Methods: A systematic search identified studies published until May 2025 using terms related
to grief, VR and other immersive technologies (i.e., augmented reality, mixed reality) from 4
databases (OVID Medline, Web of Science, PsycINFO, and Scopus). Studies reporting the use of
VR or other immersive technologies for grief were included. Intervention elements, efficacy
outcomes, acceptability and feasibility were extracted.
Results: Out of 5’704 screened titles and abstracts, 9 studies met eligibility. Types of loss
included parental loss (k=1), patient loss (k=1), loss of a spouse (k=1), gestational loss (k=1), child
loss (k=1), loss of a significant person (k=1), and loss of a person (k=3). Seven studies used a web-based
VR intervention, and two studies used a non-web-based VR intervention. VR intervention
tools included Second Life (k=2), EMMA’s WORLD (k=5), AViR (k=1) and 3MDR-TG (k=1). Our
findings show modest support for preliminary VR efficacy, with three studies showing similar
significant changes compared to control groups and five studies showing reductions in grief and
related distress outcomes. VR was further shown to be feasible and acceptable for bereaved
people.

articles_hidden.title: The Effect of an ADHD Diagnostic Label: Stigmatizing or Protective?
articles_hidden.authors: Gabrielle Geist; Ronald Auguste; Marilyn Chege; J. Bruce Morton; Ryan A Stevenson
articles_hidden.abstract: Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a highly prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by clinical symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. These symptoms are often accompanied by social stigmatization, including negative descriptors, animalistic characterizations, emotional reactions of anger, and desired social distance from individuals with ADHD. Stigmatization can negatively impact diagnosis, treatment, and behavioural functioning. This study investigates how diagnostic labels and the gender of individuals with ADHD influence stigma-related responses. Specifically, it examines whether the presence of an ADHD diagnostic label reduces or exacerbates stigma and how gender affects these perceptions. Utilizing a 2x3 factorial design, participants were presented with vignettes describing a 12-year-old child with ADHD behaviours. These vignettes varied by diagnostic label (Label vs No Label) and gender (Female, Male, and Gender-Neutral). Stigma was assessed through four outcome variables: positive-negative attitudes, humanistic-animalistic attitudes, emotional reactions, and social distance. Findings indicate that the presence of a diagnostic label significantly reduced negative attitudes, anger, and social distance. Gender effects were observed but were not statistically significant. Notably, the female vignette condition showed the strongest trends, suggesting that a diagnostic label may be particularly beneficial for females, who often go underdiagnosed. These findings highlight the potential of diagnostic labels to reduce stigma and promote social acceptance.

articles_hidden.title: Boys and Things, Girls and People?  Gender-Related Interest Patterns in Elementary School
articles_hidden.authors: Benjamin Goecke; Jessika Golle; Ingo Zettler; Ulrich Schroeders
articles_hidden.abstract: Gender-related interest patterns are well documented in adolescence and adulthood, but little is known about comparable patterns in elementary school and their relation to subject-specific interests. We assessed RIASEC-based activity preferences in 1,150 third graders in Germany (50.6% girls; mean age = 8.62 years), with interest data for 835 children approximately six months later. A 24-item version selected using T1 data showed good circumplex fit for boys and girls in temporal cross-validation at T2. Boys showed stronger things-oriented profiles (d = 0.77), whereas girls showed stronger ideas-oriented profiles (d = −0.37). The People-Things difference remained largely unchanged over six months. Domain-level retest correlations ranged from .38 to .52. Associations with academic interests were small to moderate (r = .04 to .44), whereas associations with grades were small (r = −.16 to .13). Gender-related differences in broad activity preferences are thus already visible in middle childhood, well before children make consequential educational choices.

articles_hidden.title: Object-Based Priming and the Perceived Trustworthiness of Unfamiliar Faces: A Test of Home and Work Primes
articles_hidden.authors: Oliver Bazeley
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on material priming suggests that incidental encounters with everyday objects can activate the social meanings attached to those objects and bias subsequent judgements. It remains unknown whether objects belonging to a broad social domain, such as the home or the workplace, can shift how trustworthy an unfamiliar person appears. The present study tested whether briefly viewing home-, work-, or novel-object images altered trustworthiness judgements of unfamiliar faces, predicting that home objects would raise perceived trustworthiness and work objects would lower it. Thirty adults completed a within-subjects task in which each object prime preceded a facial trustworthiness rating on a continuous 0 to 100 scale; data from 28 participants were analysed. A trial-level mixed-effects analysis found no reliable category-specific priming. Relative to novel objects, both Home (b = 2.23, 95% CI [-0.10, 4.56], p = .061) and Work (b = 2.08, 95% CI [-0.21, 4.38], p = .075) primes produced small, non-significant increases in trustworthiness, the work effect running counter to the predicted decrease. Ratings did, however, closely track normative facial trustworthiness (b = 4.61, p < .001), indicating that the task captured the intended judgement. Exploratory analyses provided one weak and non-robust indication that Home primes were stronger among Home-leaning participants, and no evidence of moderation by workplace experience. The similar effects of home and work objects may instead reflect shared familiarity or overlapping meanings. Interpretation is constrained by the modest sample, and future research should establish whether such objects reliably activate their intended constructs.

articles_hidden.title: Language and Terminology Preferences in Greek-speaking Autism Communities
articles_hidden.authors: Themis Karaminis; Despina Papoudi; Stavroula Stavrakaki
articles_hidden.abstract: The language used to discuss autism both reflects and shapes perceptions of Autistic people, yet research on terminology preferences has largely been confined to English. This study examines autism-related terminology in Greek. A sample of 1,006 Greek-speaking adults (124 Autistic adults, 434 parents/caregivers, and 448 professionals) completed an online survey, selecting, from a list of 61 terms, those they use to refer to autism, Autistic people, autism-related difficulties, and non-autistic people, and explained their choices. Data were analysed using demographics-adjusted group comparisons, principal component analysis, and thematic analysis. The groups shared a core vocabulary (“autism”, “difficulties”, “is on the autism spectrum”) but differed in their use of 39 terms, with small effects, and the main contrasts persisted after demographic adjustment. Autistic adults preferred identity-first and neurodiversity terminology, professionals favoured clinical terminology, and parents/caregivers resembled professionals on identity terms and Autistic adults on clinical terms. Identity and clinical vocabularies were independent dimensions on which every group was represented. Open-ended responses tied these choices to identity among Autistic adults, others’ reactions among parents/caregivers, and audience and setting among professionals. We discuss these findings in the context of autism research and their implications for practice and public discourse.

articles_hidden.title: Bonobos and chimpanzees: revisiting the aggression dichotomy
articles_hidden.authors: Ulrich Maloueki; Bekeli Nseu Mbomba
articles_hidden.abstract: Aggression in the genus Pan (including bonobos and chimpanzees) remains a central puzzle in primatology and anthropology. Traditionally framed as a dichotomy between “peaceful bonobos” and “violent chimpanzees,” recent findings challenge this view by documenting coalitionary aggression, maternal cannibalism, and lethal intergroup encounters in bonobos, alongside evidence that captive chimpanzees and bonobos exhibit comparable aggression levels. These observations highlight the importance of ecological context, demographic composition, and behavioral plasticity in shaping aggression. We propose that species identity is a weaker predictor of aggression in Pan than socioecological, demographic, social, and neuroendocrine context. While captivity offers methodological control, it also introduces confounds such as reduced group size, absence of fission–fusion dynamics, and enforced proximity. Conversely, wild studies reveal the ecological pressures, territorial defense, resource distribution, and interspecies competition that drive variation in aggression. Future research must integrate captive and free‑ranging data through hybrid protocols, quantify ecological and demographic drivers, and explore neuroendocrine mechanisms underlying sex‑specific aggression. An integrative review on Pan aggression will refine our understanding of adaptive strategies, illuminate the evolutionary roots of human social conflict, and advance comparative models of primate behavior.

articles_hidden.title: A Hierarchical Dynamical Model of Learning, Forgetting, and Relearning
articles_hidden.authors: Howard Smith
articles_hidden.abstract:
The model developed here provides a quantitative account of a range of well-known findings on 
learning, forgetting, and relearning, spanning delays from seconds (e.g., Peterson & Peterson, 
1959) to weeks (e.g., Ebbinghaus, 1885/1964; Perkins, 1914). The model tracks the probability of 
recall of individual items as they are learned, forgotten, and relearned over time. During study, 
recall probability increases, whereas during retention intervals it declines exponentially. Crucially, 
the rate of this decline is not fixed but is governed by a forgetting exponent that itself changes 
across study and delay periods. These changes are organised within a hierarchy of interacting 
processes operating over multiple timescales, allowing recall dynamics to evolve systematically 
across study and delay. This structure allows the model to capture effects of serial position, list 
length, spacing, and long-term retention within a single framework. Although classic studies such 
as those of Ebbinghaus, Peterson and Peterson, and Perkins are often treated as demonstrations 
of separate phenomena, the present model shows that they can be understood as arising from a 
common set of underlying processes.

articles_hidden.title: Science without scientists? In defence of human understanding
articles_hidden.authors: Jonathan Prunty
articles_hidden.abstract: Science has two grand goals, producing results and increasing human understanding, which have usually advanced together. Accelerating science by automating around human limits threatens to decouple them, as AI research output can scale with compute whereas humans can only read and digest new research at the pace biology allows, and some AI-generated results may be too opaque for anyone to follow. I argue that this could create a comprehension lag, a growing gap between what is discovered and what humans understand. This lag may begin inside individual labs, as scientists become "commissioners" directing their own teams of AI agents, but could extend to entire fields, as the frontier moves faster than people can follow. I discuss three costs of a comprehension lag: a loss of control over AI-accelerated research, a loss of capacity as aspects of training and apprenticeship are automated, and a loss of meaning that scientists find in their work. I then propose five measures to mitigate the comprehension lag, including new research directions for the cognitive and behavioural sciences, and argue that human understanding deserves protecting, both to keep oversight of AI-driven research and as an end in itself.

articles_hidden.title: Bayesian Predictive Ensembles for Random Effects Specification Uncertainty: Capturing Individual Heterogeneity in Large-Scale Assessments
articles_hidden.authors: Mingya Huang; Weicong Lyu
articles_hidden.abstract: A common challenge in multilevel modeling is determining which predictors should have random effects, especially in educational and psychological research where several theoretically plausible model specifications exist. Choosing a single specification ignores information from the alternatives and can lead to understated uncertainty in later inference. Popular Bayesian ensemble methods, including Bayesian model averaging (BMA), Bayesian stacking (BS), and Bayesian hierarchical stacking (BHS), combine predictions across candidate specifications but constrain model weights to sum to one, implicitly assuming that the candidate model set collectively accounts for all systematic variance in the outcome. This assumption rarely holds when each candidate captures only a portion of the true random effects structure. To address this, we propose to apply the Varying Coefficient Bayesian Additive Regression Tree (VCBART; Deshpande, Bai, Balocchi, Starling, & Weiss, 2024) with an adaptive intercept that absorbs variance not captured by any candidate model. The approach estimates individual-specific ensemble weights as nonparametric functions of individual-level and cluster-level covariates without imposing a sum-to-one constraint. The posterior distributions of these weights indicate which random-effects structures are most relevant for each individual and quantify the associated uncertainty. We evaluate VCBART using simulations calibrated to the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2018 mathematics data and an empirical application to the same data. Among the methods compared, VCBART achieves near-nominal prediction interval coverage with the lowest prediction error. It even outperforms the correctly specified oracle in out-of-sample prediction under high within-cluster variability.

articles_hidden.title: Longitudinal and cross-sectional perspectives on elementary school children's post-error slowing in reading and arithmetic
articles_hidden.authors: Claudia M Roebers; Daniela Menath; Hülya Özmen; Ebru Ger
articles_hidden.abstract: This study investigated the development of primary school children’s error-related adjustments in reading and arithmetic. N = 622 children from 2nd and 4th grade were tested on two tablet-based academic tasks twice in six months: an arithmetic task composed of addition and doubling items with two answer options and a silent word reading task matching words with four pictorial answer options. Children in both grades showed robust post-error slowing (PES) in both reading and arithmetic, indicating reliable monitoring and strategy use in the form of upregulating cognitive control mechanisms. Overall, post-error slowing was larger in arithmetic than in reading, independent of grade and measurement point. Fourth graders showed larger PES than 2nd graders, especially at T1, and both grades’ PES increased from T1 to T2, suggesting that task experience, improving monitoring skills, and strategy discovery play an important role. In terms of the benefits of PES for performance accuracy, PES was linked to better accuracy after the error in the arithmetic task, particularly for younger children. This was not the case for reading. Results are discussed in terms of often overlooked educationally relevant strategies in arithmetic, possible strategy’s utilization deficiency, developing monitoring and cognitive control skills in this age range and differing processing demands across academic domains.

articles_hidden.title: The Influence of Parental Cultural Values on Preschool Children's Over-Imitation
articles_hidden.authors: Esmee Miron Aalders; Moritz M. Daum; Joanna Maria Rutkowska
articles_hidden.abstract: Over-imitation, the copying of irrelevant actions, is driven by causal, affiliative, and normative processes. Because these processes develop in the environments in which children grow up, parental values likely shape them through cultural practices and interaction patterns.  Yet, how children's environments shape their over-imitation remains unexplored.
