Following the dual-process perspective \parencite{schleihauf_dual-process_2020}, this study examined whether three variables from children's environments are associated with their over-imitation of pseudo-instrumental and noncontact actions: parental cultural values, cultural diversity, and language status. We tested 133 monolingual, bilingual, and bidialectal 4-year-old children. Parents completed questionnaires on 9 dimensions of cultural values, and their child's language exposure. Two parental cultural values were associated with children’s over-imitation, but in opposite directions: Higher parental institutional collectivism was associated with less over-imitation; higher parental in-group collectivism was associated with more over-imitation. Children's language status was not associated with their over-imitation, but the distance between parents' cultural values was. Children whose parents had similar cultural values over-imitated pseudo-instrumental actions more than children whose parents' cultural values differed. Notably, cultural values were more consistently related to over-imitation of pseudo-instrumental than to noncontact actions, suggesting that preschool children do not yet apply blanket copying to pseudo-instrumental actions, or that culture has an effect above and beyond children's normative motivation to over-imitate. Overall, the results indicate that children’s over-imitation reflects both action properties and cultural environments, emphasising the importance of cultural context in theories of social learning.

articles_hidden.title: Neural evidence for intact statistical learning in Developmental Dyslexia in the absence of conclusive behavioral results: an individual differences approach to cognitive correlates
articles_hidden.authors: Iris Maria van der Wulp; Marijn Eefje Struiksma; Frank Wijnen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Individual differences in Statistical Learning (SL) are associated with reading ability, yet evidence on whether SL is impaired in Developmental Dyslexia (DD) is inconsistent. Furthermore, DD is associated with impairments in Rhythmic Ability (RA) and Working Memory (WM). This study examined SL in adults with self-reported diagnoses of DD compared to Typical Readers (TR), and explored whether individual differences in RA, WM, and vocabulary related to individual SL ability in speech segmentation.
	A total of 143 participants (N_DD = 25, N_TR = 118) were exposed to an artificial language of trisyllabic nonsense-words while neural entrainment to the words assessed SL via electroencephalography (EEG), followed by behavioral SL outcome measures. Aiming to assess individual differences, we linked the neural measure of SL to a battery of tests measuring musicality, RA, WM, and vocabulary size. 
	Results indicated neural evidence for SL in both groups, with similar neural entrainment to the structure during exposure. Behavioral performance in the DD group on SL seemed below TR, though Bayesian analyses rendered this inconclusive. The DD group obtained lower scores on tasks measuring RA, WM and vocabulary size, which was primarily driven by the latter two. Comparison of relations between neural SL and these tasks indicated no group differences therein. Exploratively combining the groups into one population resulted in anecdotal Bayesian evidence that individual differences in SL related to WM and RA measured by sensorimotor synchronization, which was rendered inconclusive in sensitivity analyses. Our results emphasize the importance of an individual differences approach, moving beyond group comparisons.

articles_hidden.title: Investigating associations between food insecurity and eating disorder pathology: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Akansha Naraindas; Georgia Pickford; Caroline West; Vivienne Hazzard; Francesca Solmi; Fidan Turk
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective
Food insecurity is increasingly recognised as an important social determinant of eating disorder (ED) pathology. Although research in this area has grown substantially, evidence remains fragmented across ED pathology, diagnoses, age groups, and clinical and non-clinical populations. This review aims to update and synthesise the literature on the relationship between food insecurity and eating disorder pathology.
Method
Relevant studies were identified by searching PubMed/Medline, Web of Science, PsycINFO, Scopus, and the grey literature up to September 2026. Random-effects meta-analyses and narrative synthesis were carried out. The methodological quality of the included studies was evaluated using Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Public and patient involvement and engagement informed the process throughout. The protocol for this review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261291381).
Results 
We included 140 articles in the review (n=628,090 participants) and, of these, 72 in the meta-analysis. Food insecurity was associated with greater overall eating pathology, with pooled eORs ranging from 1.75 (1.18–2.58) to 2.36 (0.15-0.31) across the three effect-size measures. Positive associations were also observed for binge eating, dietary restriction, purging, vomiting, and laxative use, although effect sizes varied across outcomes and analyses. Findings were mixed for excessive exercise and negative body image, with some studies reporting significant associations with food insecurity and others finding no evidence of an association. Overall, the included studies were of moderate to high methodological quality.
Conclusion
To date, the existing literature supports the role of food insecurity in the aetiology of eating disorder pathology and highlights the need for future theoretical frameworks and prevention interventions.

articles_hidden.title: Personal and National Factors Predict Depression in Europe
articles_hidden.authors: Hannes Jarke; Robin van Kessel; Kai Ruggeri; Katarzyna Czabanowska
articles_hidden.abstract: Cross-national research has consistently documented sociodemographic gradients in depression across European countries. Most comprehensive analyses, however, predate the COVID-19 pandemic and its far-reaching consequences for population mental health and social hardship. Using data from the European Social Survey Round 11 (ESS 11, collected in 2023–2024), the most recent wave to include a measure of depression (CES-D 8), we examined the social patterning of depressive symptoms across 22 EU countries and the UK (N = 39,645) using multilevel modelling with sample design weighting. We confirm findings from prior ESS rounds of consistent gender, age, and income gradients in depression, confirming their persistence in the post-pandemic period. Women reported higher depressive symptoms than men across all countries, and income emerged as the strongest individual-level predictor, with those in the lowest income tertile scoring on average 2.09 points higher on the CES-D 8 than those in the highest (the scale ranging from 0-24). Critically, these associations are not uniform across national contexts. The gender gap in depressive symptoms was larger in Southern European countries—particularly Portugal and Spain than in Northern and Eastern Europe, while the protective effect of higher income was strongest in Bulgaria, Hungary, Belgium, and Greece. Country context alone accounted for only a small proportion of total variance in depressive symptoms (ICC = 0.033), indicating that differences in depression at the population level are driven primarily by sociodemographic factors, but that their magnitude is meaningfully shaped by where people live.

articles_hidden.title: Environmental Exposures and Brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging Phenotypes in Cognitively Healthy Ageing: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Kelly E Perry; Breanna Watterson; Jenna Louise Merenstein
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Air pollution and built environment features are increasingly associated with negative health outcomes, yet their relation to brain health in cognitively healthy older adults remains unclear.

Methods: To synthesise the extant literature, we conducted a systematic review, searching MEDLINE (PubMed) and Web of Science (Core Collection) from inception to February 23, 2026. Eligible studies assessed a natural or built environmental exposure against brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) measures in cognitively healthy older adults (ages 65+). Reviewers screened and extracted summary data from published reports in Covidence; no individual patient data were sought. The main outcome was brain health; findings were synthesised narratively using an effect-direction approach, as heterogeneous exposures, outcomes, and effect metrics precluded pooling.

Findings: Of 2,496 records screened, 27 studies met eligibility, comprising >84,000 older adults across 10 countries: United States, South Korea, United Kingdom, France, Spain, Sweden, Netherlands, Taiwan, Germany, and Japan. Thirteen studies were cross-sectional and 14 were cohort studies (nine observational and five longitudinal). Higher air pollution exposure—particularly PM2.5, NO2, and PM10—was associated with altered brain structure: smaller total, grey matter, and white matter volumes, greater white matter hyperintensities, cortical thinning, and smaller medial temporal and hippocampal volumes; greenspace was associated with more favourable brain structure in several mostly cross-sectional studies, though findings were not uniform. Thirteen studies met criteria for high methodological quality and low though not uniform risk of bias; outcome assessment was a recurring source of bias (12 of 27 studies), and four of the five longitudinal studies did not meet criterion for follow-up adequacy.

Interpretation: This review synthesises emerging observational evidence that air pollution is associated with differences in brain structure in cognitively healthy ageing. Because the included evidence is predominantly cross-sectional, these associations are hypothesis generating; if confirmed in longitudinal studies, this modifiable exposure could serve as a potential target for policymakers aiming to protect brain health in the fastest growing segment of the global population.

articles_hidden.title: Processing spoken prefixed words with obscured morphological identity and boundary: An auditory masked priming experiment
articles_hidden.authors: Dave Kenneth Tayao Cayado; Samantha Wray; Adam J. Chong; Linnaea Stockall
articles_hidden.abstract: To comprehend speech, the auditory system segments a continuous input stream at various levels (e.g., sounds, words). Previous studies have shown that listeners also segment complex spoken words like treatment into their morphological units /ˈtriːt/+/mənt/, where there is a clear morphological boundary between /stem/+/affix/. Here, we report an auditory masked priming experiment in Tagalog investigating whether complex spoken words with obscured morphological identity and boundaries are segmented into morphemes. We compare the processing of prefixed words [1] without morphophonological alternations (NOCHANGE, e.g., /maŋ/+/híla/ becomes maŋhíla ‘to pull’), [2] with nasal ASSIMILATION obscuring prefix identity (e.g., /maŋ/+/búlag/ becomes mambúlag ‘to blind’), and [3] with nasal SUBSTITUTION obscuring both prefix and stem identities and their phonological boundary (e.g., /maŋ/+/túlak/ becomes manúlak ‘to push’). Crucially, these morphophonological alternations exhibit variability: nasal SUBSTITUTION is more likely for VOICELESS-initial stems than for VOICED-initial stems. We found significant priming effects of similar magnitude across NOCHANGE, ASSIMILATION, and SUBSTITUTION conditions. These effects are morphological in nature since no reliable priming was observed for monomorphemic word pairs with phonological overlap. Further, similar priming was found for both VOICELESS and VOICED SUBSTITUTION conditions. These findings unambiguously show that spoken complex words are decomposed into morphemes, thereby supporting auditory processing models and morphological theories which argue that morphologically complex words are stored and accessed as morphemes in the mental lexicon. Ultimately, we provide clear evidence that automatic decomposition in speech comprehension is robust in the face of variable morphophonological alternations that obscure prefix identity and morphological boundaries.

articles_hidden.title: “He did not want to tell me and so I did not push”: Researchers' experiences of navigating ethnographic data collection in a special school
articles_hidden.authors: Astrid Bowen; Laura Fox; Kayleigh Doyle; Kathryn Asbury
articles_hidden.abstract: Learning-disabled children and young people experience systemic barriers to their inclusion in research, and researcher expertise and experience can either act as one of those barriers or as a facilitator. Researcher accounts of conducting research with learning-disabled children and young people can provide useful insights into practices that facilitate inclusion, yet such accounts are scarce. This study presents a secondary analysis of ethnographic data collected by four researchers during a study exploring the communication preferences of learning-disabled students in a special school setting in the North of England. It focuses on the researchers’ reflections on their own experiences of data collection, as captured in their fieldnotes.  Four themes were developed using thematic analysis: (1) Moving beyond a "one size fits all" approach; (2) The importance of relationships; (3) Researching as an outsider/insider; (4) Why it matters who does the research. Findings highlight the positive, yet sometimes challenging, experiences of working with learning-disabled students in a special school setting, and contribute to the knowledge base on supporting inclusive practices for qualitative research with learning-disabled participants. Suggestions for how researchers can develop strategies to navigate the challenges they may encounter during data collection are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Perioral motor stabilization without classical proprioception: a trigeminofacial force-balance model
articles_hidden.authors: Thomas Quettier; Paola Sessa; Luigi Cattaneo; Pier Francesco Ferrari
articles_hidden.abstract: Voluntary perioral movements, including speech articulation, deliberate lip posturing, and postural stabilization during oral closure, require motor precision despite the absence of muscle spindles and proprioceptive receptors in perioral musculature. The facial nerve is purely efferent, providing no direct sensory return. How the motor system achieves stable control under these constraints has remained unresolved. We propose the Orofacial Region as Integrated System (ORIS) model as a mechanistic candidate tailored to voluntary and automatic segmental perioral behaviors. The model identifies cutaneous mechanoreception via the trigeminal nerve as the primary afferent channel for perioral motor stabilization and proposes that the controlled variable is the spatial equilibrium of dermal surface tension across the perioral sheet, monitored by slowly and fast-adapting mechanoreceptors concentrated in the perioral region. The orbicularis oris sphincter provides circumferential tensile stability against which directional muscles act, with the modiolus anguli oris serving as the primary force-transmission junction. Three testable predictions follow from this architecture. Clinical implications for facial motor rehabilitation are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Recognizing versus valuing curiosity: Cross-country similarities and differences in parental judgments of early curious behaviors
articles_hidden.authors: Elena C. Altmann; Lizhi Ma; Mikako Ishibashi; Yaying (Tiffany) Bai; Keiya Taguchi; Gert Westermann; Hiromichi Hagihara
articles_hidden.abstract: Cross-cultural research has examined whether parents differ in how they value curiosity as a developmental characteristic, but it remains unclear whether they understand the concept in the same way. Because early curiosity must be inferred from behavior, concrete behavioral judgments offer a direct test of this question. Parents in Germany, China, and Japan were randomly assigned to judge age-appropriate behaviors from a published infant-toddler or early-childhood curiosity measure, rating each either as an expression of curiosity or as socially desirable. The 689 parents (142 German, 425 Chinese, and 122 Japanese; ethnicity not explicitly collected) reported on children aged 5 to 71 months (344 girls, 345 boys) between July 2025 and March 2026. Candidate curiosity items clearly outperformed non-curiosity fillers in every country (differences of 1.19 to 2.84 points on a 7-point scale), and behavior orderings were strongly similar across countries (Spearman ρ = .67 to .88). Ratings were near-identical for individual items such as poking and probing, with country differences in curiosity attribution occurring much less compared to desirability differences (for 4 versus 19 items). These findings suggest that cultures may differ less in what curiosity looks like than in which behavioral expressions of curiosity are welcomed and reinforced.

articles_hidden.title: Multiplying Bayes Factors Across Studies: Which Hypotheses Are We Testing?
articles_hidden.authors: Laura Groot; Daniel W. Heck
articles_hidden.abstract: Bayesian evidence synthesis (BES) is a method for evaluating the empirical support for a common theory across multiple studies. In each study, the theory predicts a set of order constraints on the parameters of interest. Evidence is aggregated by multiplying the Bayes factors of the individual studies, yielding the product Bayes factor (PBF). The numerator of the PBF corresponds to the joint predicted hypothesis that the theory holds across different contexts, implying that the predicted order constraints are correct in each study. Since the Bayes factor is a relative measure of evidence, interpreting the PBF requires a clear understanding of the alternative hypothesis. The joint alternative is represented by the denominator of the PBF and states that the respective study-specific alternative hypothesis holds in each study. However, this joint alternative may lack both a clear substantive interpretation and a theoretical justification. We investigate how different combinations of study-specific alternative hypotheses give rise to distinct joint alternatives, focusing on three alternatives common in order-constrained inference: the null, the unconstrained, and the complement hypothesis. In particular, we show that multiplying Bayes factors involving study-specific complements does not test the theory against its complement (i.e., the hypothesis that the theoretical predictions are false in at least one study). Finally, we provide recommendations for specifying meaningful joint alternative hypotheses that support a clear interpretation of BES results and are useful for theory testing.

articles_hidden.title: The Association between Climate Anxiety and Nature Connectedness: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Angus D. E. Faul; Léan V. O’Brien; Teaghan Hogg
articles_hidden.abstract:
Nature connectedness (NC) refers to an individual’s subjective sense of connection with nature and has a well-established link to overall health and well-being. NC shows potential for being incorporated into future climate anxiety (CA) management interventions. However, no study has reviewed the literature investigating the association between NC and CA. Therefore, we conducted a systematic literature review to: 1) synthesise the empirical research and assess the evidence for associations between NC and CA using meta-analytic methods; and 2) identify factors that may influence this relationship, and the nature of their influence. Following a systematic search of eight electronic databases from inception to April 2026, fifty studies met inclusion criteria. Substantial heterogeneity was identified in NC and CA operationalisations. We conducted random-effects meta-analyses using restricted maximum likelihood estimation (REML), using correlation coefficients (r) as the effect size metric and pooled across studies using inverse-variance weighting. Meta-analysis indicated a significant positive moderate mean association between NC and CA. NC and CA measurement instruments/items were selected as categorical moderators. Subgroup analyses revealed 15 CA instruments significantly influenced the relationship between NC and CA. Based on our findings we recommend: (a) the development and refinement of CA instruments and their conceptual alignment, (b) more diverse population contexts in this research area, and (c) the development of a clear theoretical framework for defining and conceptualising NC and its relationship with CA. This review was registered on the PROSPERO International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (Registration ID = CRD420251063755). 
Keywords: Nature connectedness (NC), climate anxiety (CA), meta-analysis, measures, operationalisations.

articles_hidden.title: Which Distortion gets confused? A Controlled Comparison of Language Models for Dominant Cognitive Distortion Classification
articles_hidden.authors: Rishi Gnanasekar; Caleb J. Siefert
articles_hidden.abstract:
Cognitive Distortions are unhelpful thinking
patterns that Cognitive Behavioral Therapy
(CBT) aims to identify and restructure, so
classifying cognitive distortions is a crucial
process for reframing. The classification
becomes difficult as the data is limited, and
the data are imbalanced most of the time. We
study dominant distortion classification on
the publicly available Therapist Q&A dataset
(Shreevastava and Foltz, 2021) where the anno-
tator agreement on the dominant distortion is
low (34%). Using the annotated distorted span
as input, we compare TF-IDF baselines with
RoBERTa, DeBERTa-v3 and MentalBERT
(with and without focal loss) over three seeds,
reporting accuracy, macro F1 and Cohen’s
kappa with significance tests. The encoders
reach 0.39 to 0.44 accuracy, well above the
majority-class baseline (0.15), the three cross-
entropy encoders are not significantly different
from each other, while the weighted focal loss
is worse. An error analysis shows that errors
concentrate on a small group of overlapping
distortions, mainly All-or-nothing thinking,
Magnification and Mental filter, which
suggests that unclear category boundaries limit
performance more than model choice.

articles_hidden.title: The social ecology of trustworthiness inferences: Cultural gradients in emotion overgeneralization
articles_hidden.authors: Yuqing Shi; Ryutaro Uchiyama; Shuxian Jin; Yin Wang; Steve M. J. Janssen; Daniel DongWon Oh
articles_hidden.abstract: Judgments of trustworthiness from faces guide critical social decisions. It remains debated whether these judgments reflect shared features of human perception or are shaped by cultural experience. One prominent explanation is emotion overgeneralization: faces that structurally resemble emotional expressions elicit corresponding impressions, even when no emotion is displayed. Although often treated as universal, emotion overgeneralization may reflect ecological learning shaped by culture-specific norms. We propose a cultural gradient: where emotional expressions are more informative, the link between happiness resemblance and perceived trustworthiness should be stronger. Participants from 32 countries (N ≈ 6,400) will evaluate the trustworthiness of unfamiliar individuals from standardized resting facial photographs and complete a measure of emotional expressivity, with each face’s resemblance to happiness quantified computationally. We will test whether emotional expressivity is associated with greater emotion overgeneralization at both country and individual levels. Null results would favor perceptual invariance, whereas positive associations would support ecological calibration.

articles_hidden.title: Tracking vocabulary development as children start school: assessing measurement invariance in multilingual classrooms
articles_hidden.authors: Sonali Nag; Athina Ntalli; Gideon Arulmani; Joshua Aaron McGrane
articles_hidden.abstract: Receptive vocabulary, what is understood when hearing a word, underpins reading comprehension and wider learning. Yet, few tests have been validated to function fairly over developmental time and across diverse linguistic experiences. This study examined the Picture Test for Receptive Vocabulary (TalkTogether – Hindi), a 50-item test for four-to-nine-year-olds in multilingual north India. Words in the language of school instruction and linked images were drawn picture- and story books. Over one academic year (2023–2024), 1,949 administrations were collected from children (47% girls) at three time points across 40 schools. The test showed good reliability (Cronbach’s α = .82; Rasch reliability = .78) and captured variation across the proficiency range. Item properties remained stable across time, licensing its use as a fair tracking tool. Between-group differential item functioning (DIF) effects—by sex, home language(s), and a novel index of ambient peer language exposure—were small to negligible. The findings demonstrate that a contextually-situated vocabulary test, validated through rigorous psychometric evaluation, can meet the standards required for fair tracking of oral skills in the language of instruction. The reported protocol to inform item revision and evaluate dimensions of measurement invariance—demographic, contextual and developmental—are likely transferable to other similarly multilingual settings.

articles_hidden.title: An introduction to longitudinal multilevel and structural equation modeling approaches for examining change
articles_hidden.authors: Razieh Pourafshari; Miriam Brinberg; Joseph Bayer
articles_hidden.abstract: This chapter provides a practical introduction to two statistical frameworks for analyzing longitudinal data in quantitative communication research: multilevel modeling (MLM) and structural equation modeling (SEM). Focusing on intraindividual change and intraindividual variability, we illustrate how these methods can disentangle within-person processes from between-person differences. Using real-world data, the chapter demonstrates how to model daily patterns in social interaction desires and test dynamic relationships between social app use and interpersonal needs. Key considerations for choosing between MLM and SEM are discussed. The chapter also highlights advanced extensions, including nonlinear growth, mediation, and multivariate models, offering researchers a foundational guide for applying these approaches to their own questions examining change.

articles_hidden.title: From transdiagnostic compulsivity to clinical applications: a computational psychiatry approach to bridge research and clinic
articles_hidden.authors: Sean E Cavanagh; Toby Wise
articles_hidden.abstract: Compulsivity, the maladaptive persistence of behaviour despite adverse consequences, is central to obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and has been increasingly conceptualised as a transdiagnostic dimension spanning multiple neuropsychiatric disorders. Research within computational psychiatry has linked dimensional compulsivity to two candidate mechanisms: impaired goal-directed control and elevated metacognitive confidence. Here, we take a clinical perspective addressing how insights from these findings can be brought into practice. We first ask how dimensional compulsivity measures should be interpreted with respect to clinical presentations and discuss conflicts between the general population findings and clinical data. We highlight several challenges facing clinical implementation: effect sizes are small, goal-directed control has not been shown to change with either pharmacotherapy or psychological therapy, and the overconfidence associated with dimensional compulsivity contrasts with the reduced confidence reported in patients with OCD. We argue these discrepancies are informative rather than disqualifying and set out a translational roadmap for mechanistically informed detection and transdiagnostic intervention. Specifically, we suggest that screening and digital monitoring of dimensional compulsivity, combined with cognitive and mechanistic phenotyping to guide psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy, may ultimately improve outcomes across diagnostic boundaries.

articles_hidden.title: The Governed Heart:  Institutional Emotion Regulation through Policy, Proclamation, and Proxy
articles_hidden.authors: Nicholas Paul Camp; Brett Quaid Ford
articles_hidden.abstract: Governments, schools, hospitals, companies, and myriad other organizations structure institutional life and mobilize large numbers of people to accomplish what they cannot do alone. Institutions also regulate something less visible, but equally consequential: the emotions of their constituents. We introduce institutional emotion regulation as the formal processes by which institutions, through organizations, seek to influence the emotions people have, when they have them, and how they experience and express these emotions. Research across the social sciences has examined how particular organizations attempt to shape affective experiences, but these literatures have largely developed in disciplinary silos or domain-specific settings. We propose that these phenomena reflect a distinct level of emotion regulation, characterized by emotion goals held by organizations and pursued through formal institutional means. We develop a framework that crosses four established stages of emotion regulation – targeting situations, attention, appraisals, and responses – with three distinctive vectors of institutional influence: policies, the rules and structures that shape people’s environments; proclamations, communications directed toward the public; and proxies, the agents who act on behalf of the organization. Our framework provides a common language for understanding how institutions influence emotional life at scale and suggests novel directions for psychological study while surfacing broader questions for society around the appropriate use of this influence.

articles_hidden.title: Simulated Survival: A Theoretical Framework for Using Immersive Virtual Reality Challenge to Target Ideation-to-Action Mechanisms of Suicide Risk
articles_hidden.authors: Mohammad Sheraz Akbar; Fatima Afsar
articles_hidden.abstract: Ideation-to-action theories explain how suicidal desire develops and how some people come to act on it, but they give little guidance on interventions for the physiological state that accompanies suicidal crises. This article proposes Simulated Survival, a theoretical framework for using controlled, demanding experiences in immersive virtual reality (VR) as an adjunct to suicide-specific care. Drawing on the Three-Step Theory, the Integrated Motivational-Volitional model, and the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide, together with research on autonomic regulation, interoception, attention under pressure, challenge appraisal, adventure-based interventions, and VR, the framework specifies three hypothesized mechanisms: interruption of suicide-specific rumination through attention captured by demanding, embodied tasks; repeated stress-recovery cycles that train autonomic and interoceptive regulation; and the pairing of high arousal with successful protective action, intended to strengthen self-preservation rather than tolerance of death-related fear. Expectation violation is proposed as the learning process that turns short-term effects into lasting change. Because repeated exposure to danger could raise fearlessness about death, the framework sets design rules (no suicide-method cues, no virtual death states, graded difficulty) and treats fearlessness about death as a primary safety outcome. Eight testable propositions and a staged research path are set out. Simulated Survival offers a testable basis for body-based digital interventions in suicide prevention, and its value depends on experimental work that tests each mechanism against active VR control conditions before any clinical trial.

articles_hidden.title: Children adjust behavior in novel social environments to reflect local prosocial norms inferred from brief exposure
articles_hidden.authors: Kari Britt Schroeder; Laura Nelson; Peter Blake
articles_hidden.abstract: Stark cultural variation in prosocial behavior, as elicited with economic experiments, is evident despite the high mobility of humans. Conformity to local norms has been posited to play an integral role in the maintenance of this variation. Experiments suggest that adults indeed rapidly infer pro- and antisocial norms in new or altered social environments and adjust their behavior to reflect the inferred norms. Studies of the ontogeny of prosocial behavior show that by middle childhood, children’s prosocial behavior conforms to that of local adults. Furthermore, by this stage, children are susceptible to the manipulation of explicit normative information. However, their propensity to extract or infer normative information from the environment and change their behavior accordingly has not been investigated. Here, we assess whether children 1) rapidly infer local prosocial norms in a novel, realistic social environment, 2) extend these inferences to norms for unobserved behaviors, and 3) alter their behavior in the novel environment to align with the inferred norms while still 4) maintaining their baseline prosocial behavior outside of the novel environment. We used questionnaires to measure children’s perceived pro- and antisocial descriptive norms in their Own Neighborhoods as well as in a novel “Neighborhood X,” to which they were introduced via a slideshow. Norms for Neighborhood X diverged drastically dependent upon which slideshow they witnessed (Prosocial or Antisocial condition), a result robust to the exclusion of questions about norms for behaviors observed in the slideshow. Children’s perceptions of prosocial norms in their Own Neighborhoods predicted their prosocial behavior (Dictator Game) in their Own Neighborhood. Moreover, even though information about giving behavior was not presented in the slideshow, inferred norms for Neighborhood X predicted children’s prosocial behavior in that neighborhood as well. These changes in prosocial behavior were transitory and specific to Neighborhood X; prosocial behavior in a separate “Helping Task” was best predicted by prosocial norms within the children’s Own Neighborhoods. Our results are consistent with the hypothesis that humans have a propensity to rapidly infer and conform to local prosocial norms, thus maintaining group differences in prosocial behavior, and further indicate that this propensity is in operation by middle childhood.

articles_hidden.title: Multilingualism WithOut Words: A non-lexicalist model of bilingualism
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandra Krauska; Danielle Fahey
articles_hidden.abstract: Standard models of bilingualism are primarily concerned with how words in multiple languages are stored and associated in the mind. However, there is growing consensus in linguistic theory that language cannot be organized around words, given that meaning, syntax, and form do not always align at the word level. We propose the Multilingualism WithOut Words (M-WOW) model to realign models of bilingualism with current linguistic theory and account for a broader typology of languages. In contrast to other models, M-WOW allows more flexibility in how features are realized across languages and expands the possibilities for code-switching. Because the model does not rely on a word level, it accommodates a broader set of linguistic phenomena and provides new insights into bilingual language processing and the dynamic and variable processes of L2 acquisition and attrition.

articles_hidden.title: Noun memory advantage drives sentence internal primacy and recency at clause boundaries
articles_hidden.authors: Sebastián Mancha; Ellen Lau
articles_hidden.abstract: Classic research in psychology has shown that comprehenders in recall tasks ‘chunk’ word lists in order to facilitate later retrieval. Here we ask how chunking mechanisms apply in grammatically structured sentence stimuli. How do comprehenders make use of this grammatical structure to guide chunking of a sentence’s component words in memory? In previous studies of multi-clause sentence recall, many researchers have argued that chunking is clause-based, as evidenced by scalloped serial accuracy curves in which primacy and recency effects are observed within each clause. Here we suggest that these previous findings may have been driven by the correlation of sentence boundaries with nouns, a lexical class known to demonstrate an independent accuracy advantage in recall. Using immediate serial recall of naturalistic biclausal English sentences and manipulating noun placement, we find evidence that nouns indeed confer a large accuracy boost at the internal clause boundary that can explain prior results. We discuss the difficulty of applying serial position logic to highly structured representations such as those that underlie sentence forms.

articles_hidden.title: A Placebo Cannot Be Psychedelic: Why psychedelic trials need dose, not mimicry, as their control
articles_hidden.authors: Wolfgang Liedtke
articles_hidden.abstract: In a recently published Viewpoint, Yang-et-al propose masking high-dose psilocybin trials with a multidrug comparator engineered to reproduce the psychedelic experience. Their objective, restoration of the gold-standard of randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled standard, is well-intentioned, but the proposed approach dissolves the concept it aims to rescue. A placebo permits to understand the impact of expectation because it is inert. Recent neural circuit-level results in mice shows how concretely expectation affects behavior, relying on in-vivo experimentation that separates placebo effect from active treatment. A comparator that recreates the psychedelic experience must engage the circuits that generate it, becoming a second active treatment whose own pharmacology confounds any eventual difference placebo-active, possibly in both directions. Some interventions, from topical TRP-channel activators (capsaicin, menthol) to classic psychedelics, cannot be matched by an inert control. Dose-controlled designs represent the remaining option where well-intentioned mimicry fails: their main possible bias might work against the drug. Dose-controlled designs can be paired with external controls and approval tied to mandatory postmarketing evidence.

articles_hidden.title: Comparing Logit and Probit Coefficients From Same-Sample Nested Models: Adapting the (Revised) KHB Method to an SEM Framework
articles_hidden.authors: Wolfgang Wagner; Benjamin Nagengast
articles_hidden.abstract: Karlson et al. (2012) suggested an estimation strategy for logistic and probit regression models, the so-called KHB method, which allows differences between regression coefficients in same-sample nested regression models to be interpreted. We introduce the pseudo mediation model (PMM), which implements the KHB method in a structural equation modeling (SEM) framework. The PMM has several advantages over the “standard” KHB method: First, missing data can be handled under less restrictive assumptions. Second, predictors can be included as latent variables to avoid bias due to measurement error. Finally, nested data structures and survey weights can be accounted for. We illustrate the method with empirical examples.

articles_hidden.title: A systematic review of recruitment and retention within randomised controlled trials of adults with Down Syndrome
articles_hidden.authors: Aimee Wilkinson; Jade Eloise Norris; Nicola Mills; Victoria Nimmo-Smith; Angela Hassiotis; Dheeraj Rai; Alba X Realpe
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Adults with Down Syndrome (DS) face significant health inequalities. Evidence from high-quality randomised controlled trials (RCTs) for interventions are lacking, and there is a perceived difficulty regarding recruiting and retaining participants with DS. 
Aims: This systematic review aimed to examine planned vs. actual recruitment and retention rates of RCTs involving adults with DS, summarising reported facilitators of and barriers to participation.
Method: MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and EMBASE databases were searched systematically to retrieve RCTs of any intervention involving adults with DS =>16yrs, published to 07/12/2023, with a second search in April 2025. Searches were also conducted on trial registries, and reference lists reviewed. Trial design, planned and achieved sample size, retention rate, and recruitment and retention strategies were extracted 26/02/2024-18/03/2024 for the first search, and in August 2025 for the updated search (Prospero: CRD42023447126; registered: 04/09/2023). 
Results: After deduplication, 1,622 articles underwent title and abstract screening, with 89 full texts reviewed. Five additional papers were identified from reference lists. 1,785 adults with DS were randomised to 44 included RCTs. Most studies did not pre-register their protocol nor target sample size (n=16 reported target N; 36.36%) and typically recruited small samples: 13 recruited N ≥40 (29.55%; N range=8-337, median N=25, IQR 21.75). Attrition by primary outcome also varied widely (0-47%).
Conclusions: There is a paucity of high-quality, large-scale RCTs involving adults with DS, and challenges related to participation rates (e.g., stringent exclusion criteria, consent challenges, and study burden). Strategies to overcome challenges in recruitment and retention to such trials are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: How do time of day and location influence affect experience? A passive sensing study
articles_hidden.authors: Simon M. Li; Molly Patapoff; Aanika Schueler; Qimin Liu; David E. Gard; Carlos Busso; Jukka-Pekka Onnela; Daniel Fulford
articles_hidden.abstract: Momentary emotional experience is shaped by the contexts in which individuals are embedded, yet little is known about how time spent in certain locations (e.g., at home versus in public spaces) relates to affect in daily life. In the current study, 74 young adults completed 14 days of smartphone-based ecological momentary assessment and GPS-based geolocation. We examined three contextual dimensions in relation to momentary affect (happiness, anxiety, and sadness) in young adults: environmental context (at home versus outside), recent exposure duration (time spent at home in the preceding three hours), and temporal context (time of day and day of week). Multilevel models indicated that participants reported higher happiness and lower anxiety in the evening relative to morning, and higher happiness on weekends than on weekdays. Within individuals, being at home (and time spent at home) was associated with lower happiness than being outside the home. Furthermore, the exploratory analysis suggested that the association between time spent at home and lower happiness was stronger among individuals who typically spent less time at home. These findings suggest that temporal and environmental contexts are associated with momentary happiness, whereas environmental context was not associated with anxiety or sadness.

articles_hidden.title: Humans adaptively delay planning using cognitive maps
articles_hidden.authors: Paul B. Sharp; Eran Eldar
articles_hidden.abstract: Planning is an expensive computational operation that easily exhausts our cognitive resources. For this reason, it is critical to learn strategies to initiate planning wisely. To understand how humans adaptively initiate planning, we developed a task where humans can learn to delay planning at certain timepoints when all actions are equally likely to reach an instructed goal. Across two pre-registered studies, we show that humans adaptively delay planning, and improve in their ability to do so with experience. To explain this behavior, we formalize a model of the underlying meta-control computations. Our model demonstrates how strategies to delay planning are not learned from experienced outcomes, but rather, from searching a cognitive map of the task to determine at which points it is more valuable to delay control. We thus establish that humans can adaptively delay planning, and learn to do so by means of a cognitive map.

articles_hidden.title: Perceptual distinctiveness underlies apparent emotion-specific advantages in facial expression detection
articles_hidden.authors: Erika Bucci; Giacomo Handjaras; Giada Lettieri; Luca Cecchetti
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans are assumed to prioritize facial expressions because of the evolutionary significance of their affective content. Here, we show that this assumption does not survive rigorous control of perceptual structure. Across three studies integrating preregistered visual search experiments, geometric modeling of facial expressions, and eye-tracking data, we tested whether detection advantages for happy and angry faces reflect low-level visual salience rather than emotion. To this end, we combined frequentist interval testing with a predefined smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) and Bayesian region-of-practical-equivalence (ROPE) analyses. Behavioral and oculomotor measures reliably predicted emotion category when expressions were presented at full, perceptually unbalanced intensity. By contrast, when expression intensity was matched, both interval testing and Bayesian ROPE analyses supported the absence of a practically meaningful effect. In addition, detection speed and accuracy were best explained by geometric deviation from a neutral face, independent of emotional category. These findings indicate that apparent emotion advantages in visual search arise from perceptual salience rather than privileged access to emotion, challenging evolutionary accounts of attentional prioritization.

articles_hidden.title: Child Multilingualisms Beyond WEIRD Contexts: Evidence from Asia and Africa
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandra Paquette; Leher Singh
articles_hidden.abstract: Who is the language learner represented in language acquisition research? Despite the prevalence and diversity of multilingual childhoods, theories of early language development remain grounded in monolinguals from Euro-American contexts, while multilingual research has concentrated on limited populations/settings. This review examines multilingual language development during the first three years across Asia and Africa, attending to diversity within and between regions. Research on input, speech perception, word recognition, and vocabulary indicate that multilingual infants flexibly adapt to linguistic ecologies, but vary in developmental pathways. We argue that multilingualism should be conceptualized not as a categorical characteristic, but as a multidimensional ecology structured by language combinations, caregiving arrangements, social functions, socioeconomic conditions, and colonial histories. We conclude with a research agenda that broadens empirical and linguistic coverage, improves measurement of multilingual experiences, and centers community-informed priorities. A globally adequate science of language development requires building theory from children’s diverse multilingual realities.

articles_hidden.title: Evaluating the Parental Burnout Assessment in parents of children with and without complex care needs: Measurement invariance, group differences, and the correlates of sociodemographic characteristics
articles_hidden.authors: Nathalie Patty; Caro Henrica Catharina Lemmen; Carlo Schuengel; Karen van Meeteren; Marjolijn Ketelaar; Maartje Luijk; Agnes M. Willemen
articles_hidden.abstract: The study aim was to evaluate the measurement invariance of the Parental Burnout Assessment (PBA), across parents of children with complex care needs (CCN) and parents of children without CCN, compare burnout scores between these groups, and explore how sociodemographic characteristics relate to parental burnout within each parenting context. The PBA was completed by 337 parents of children with CCN and 329 parents who did not have a child with CCN. Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) supported the theoretically proposed four-factor structure of the PBA, encompassing exhaustion in the parental role, feelings of being fed up, contrast with pervious parental self, and emotional distancing. A subsequent second-order CFA indicated that these four dimensions could be explained by a single overarching factor, parental burnout. Multigroup CFA supported scalar invariance across groups for both the four-factor model and the second-order model, indicating that the observed group differences in PBA scores reflect true differences rather than measurement bias. Parents of children with CCN reported significantly higher PBA scores than parents of children without CCN (d = 1.33, p < .001). Among the sociodemographic characteristics examined, we found that being a mother of a child with CCN was associated with substantially higher PBA scores compared to being a father of a child with CCN. This gender difference was smaller among parents of children without CCN. Parental age, ethnicity, educational attainment, being single parent, the number of children, and minimum and maximum age of the child were not associated with higher parental burnout scores. Findings underscore the heightened vulnerability for parental burnout among parents of children with CCN compared to parents of children without CCN while also providing further evidence for the suitability of the PBA as a research instrument for assessing parental burnout across the caregiving context of being a parent of a child with CCN or not.

articles_hidden.title: Mapping Leadership in Teams: An Empirically Grounded Taxonomy of Formal and Peer Leadership Roles.
articles_hidden.authors: Charlotte Marie Edelmann; Filip Boen; Jeroen Stouten; Katrien Fransen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: Formal and peer (informal) leaders play crucial roles in fostering team effectiveness and member well-being. Although leadership research has examined a wide range of leader behaviors, it remains fragmented and typically focuses on either formal or peer leaders rather than both. Moreover, no empirically grounded taxonomy captures the breadth of leadership behaviors across hierarchical levels.

Design/methodology/approach: To address this gap, we developed an inductively derived, literature-integrated taxonomy of leadership functions. We first conducted qualitative interviews with 35 employees varying in hierarchical level, education, sector, and gender. Qualitative content analysis identified leadership functions enacted by formal and peer leaders. Participants then completed individual and group card-sorting exercises to cluster these functions into higher-order leadership roles.

Findings: The taxonomy comprised 10 formal and 10 peer leadership roles. Comparison with existing leadership frameworks showed where prior research converges with and extends the leadership functions identified by participants.

Originality: This integrative taxonomy provides a practice-informed framework for advancing leadership theory and informing leadership development across organizational contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Testing Socio-Perceptual Equigenesis with Biophilic Interventions: A Virtual Reality Eye-Tracking Study Across Neighborhood Socioeconomic Status
articles_hidden.authors: Paula Latorre; Cleiton Pons Ferreira; Aurora Molina-Muñoz; Sergio Castaño-Castaño; Miguel Morales Navas; Francisco Nieto-Escamez
articles_hidden.abstract:
Inequity in access to urban green spaces perpetuates marked disparities in psychological well-being in cities. The present study evaluates whether micro-scale biophilic interventions in virtual environments act as a socio-perceptual equalizer (Environmental Equigenesis Hypothesis) and modulate attention through oculomotor patterns of soft fascination (Attention Restoration Theory). Within this framework, 60 Hz eye-tracking integrated into Immersive Virtual Reality (IVR) was used to capture implicit attentional dynamics objectively. Framed within a mixed methods project registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF) after data collection and before any inferential analysis, and given the density of the data obtained, this manuscript reports exclusively the quantitative block focused on oculomotor and psychometric triangulation, reserving the qualitative analysis for a subsequent report. A sample of 75 participants exposed to 360° virtual tours evaluated low-, medium-, and high-socioeconomic-status (SES) neighborhoods under Original and Enhanced conditions. Eye-tracking revealed that the biophilic design did not alter the total volume of fixations but significantly reduced the average fixation duration, a pattern compatible with the attentional coupling of soft fascination. In parallel, subjective increases in positive affect, liking, esthetic evaluation, and relaxation were observed, while perceived stress did not change significantly overall. No significant differences in esthetic evaluation between neighborhoods remained after the intervention, and the areas-of-interest (AOIs) metrics showed a different allocation of gaze across neighborhoods, partly because the interventions applied were not the same in each one. Eye-tracking complemented the self-report data, although the main equigenesis findings rest on the psychometric measures.
Keywords: virtual reality, eye-tracking, biophilic design, attention restoration theory, environmental equigenesis, socioeconomic status

articles_hidden.title: Don’t throw the baby out with the bathwater! Why "preregistration" is still a useful term: Commentary on Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025)
articles_hidden.authors: Priya Silverstein; Lisa Spitzer; Lukas Wallrich; Josefina Weinerova
articles_hidden.abstract: This is a commentary on Mayo-Wilson et al. (2025), published in Avances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science (AMPPS). As per AMPPS submission guidelines, no abstract is included for commentaries.

articles_hidden.title: How Self-Location Predicts the Degree and Quality of the Felt Sense of Connection
articles_hidden.authors: MARIE SESTER; Glenn Hartelius; Michaël Dambrun
articles_hidden.abstract: Research has typically examined how self-location in the head or heart is associated with traits and behavior, yet its link to relationality—specifically the felt sense of connection—remains underexplored. This study investigated how dispositional self-location predicts the embodied experience of being relationally linked to others and the world. We initially developed the Dispositional Self-Location Questionnaire (DSLQ), an association-based instrument designed to minimize potential subjective bias in participant reporting of self-location. Using this measure, we categorized a U.S. sample of 218 adults who had reported a strong experience of connection as head-locators or heart-locators and assessed them on self-construal, self-expansiveness, connectedness, and perceived qualities of connection. Head-locators reported firmer self-boundaries, emphasizing independence, rationality, and decision-making. In contrast, Heart-locators scored significantly higher on connectedness to both self and world, and on metapersonal self-construal, describing their connections as close, warm, caring, and authentic. These findings suggest that self-location functions as a somatic attentional stance that anticipates the experiential boundary between self and other: the head favors separation and autonomy, while the heart favors openness and expanded belonging.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive Polyphasia and Cognitive Dissonance: An Integrative Model for Understanding Inconsistency Management Within Social Representations Theory
articles_hidden.authors: Thiago Mikael Silva; Adriano Roberto Afonso do Nascimento
articles_hidden.abstract:
The aim of this study was to explore the interrelationship between cognitive
polyphasia and cognitive dissonance in the management of contradictions. We argue
that both concepts maintain a circular relationship. To support this position, we
establish a theoretical path structured around four core axes: 1) the recognition that
Festinger and his followers already considered dissonance management mechanisms
that, much like cognitive polyphasia, maintain inconsistency; 2) from a diachronic
perspective, dissonance can stem from cognitive polyphasia; 3) from a synchronic
perspective, the varieties of cognitive polyphasia can be systematized within the
functional approach to cognitive dissonance; 4) this systematization raises questions
regarding the self and identity, bringing Social Representations Theory closer to
contemporary models of the self. Throughout this path, we outline an integrative
model for the study of inconsistency management, offering brief considerations on the
challenges that future research must overcome.

articles_hidden.title: It’s about time: Specifying time zero for target trial emulation in psychological research
articles_hidden.authors: Dongning Ren; Wen Wei Loh
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychologists often rely on observational studies for causal evidence, which raises the question of how to strengthen the design of observational studies for causal inference. One widely used approach in medical research is target trial emulation (TTE). In this tutorial, we introduce TTE to psychological research, with particular emphasis on its cornerstone concept that is routinely ignored in practice: time zero. Following a brief primer on TTE, we foreground time zero and highlight its critical role in improving valid causal inferences from observational data. Using examples drawn from psychological research, we systematically enumerate all possible permutations of the time zero components to show how their misalignment can introduce systematic biases, including selection bias, post-treatment confounding, treatment-dependent (in)eligibility, and immortal time bias, even when all baseline confounders are measured. To address this, we develop a decision framework for integrating time zero into research practices and offer practical recommendations. Through a running example of workplace AI use and employee burnout, we demonstrate how clearly specifying time zero clarifies causal questions, prevents many design-based biases, and strengthens internal validity. We further emphasize that time zero alignment is only one design feature of a strong observational study, and we delineate the boundaries of TTE, cautioning against the misconception that it is a magic fix that automatically delivers causal conclusions. We conclude that explicitly justifying time zero is a necessary step toward improving the rigor and transparency of causal research in psychology.

articles_hidden.title: Mediterranean-style dietary components and self-reported depression: a cross-sectional analysis of 502,359 UK adults in the UK Biobank cohort
articles_hidden.authors: Haidi Martinidou; Donald M Lyall
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Mediterranean-style diet adherence has been associated with lower depression prevalence, but studies are typically small and adjust for few confounders. We aimed to estimate cross-sectional associations between individual Mediterranean-style dietary components and reported depression, and how far they attenuate with broader sociodemographic and lifestyle adjustment.
Methods: Cross-sectional analysis of the UK Biobank cohort (N=502,359). Six self-reported dietary variables - oily fish, non-oily fish, fresh fruit, salad and raw vegetables, cooked vegetables and processed meat - were tested against self-reported depression using binary logistic regression, modelled individually with progressive adjustment (full adjustment: age, sex, smoking, medication, Townsend deprivation index, month of assessment, educational attainment), then all together in one multivariable model.
Results: 28,194 participants (5.6%) reported depression. Fully adjusted, higher intakes of oily fish (odds ratio[OR]=0.900, 95% CI [confidence intervals] 0.888 to 0.912), non-oily fish (OR=0.931, 0.917 to 0.945), fresh fruit (OR=0.974, 0.966 to 0.982), salad and raw vegetables (OR=0.970, 0.964 to 0.976) and cooked vegetables (OR=0.967, 0.960 to 0.974) were each associated with lower odds. 
Conclusion: Individual components of a Mediterranean-style diet showed small, consistent associations with lower odds of self-reported depression, not explained by the measured confounders. The design does not support causal interpretation. For researchers, prospective designs with repeated dietary measurement and diagnosed outcomes are needed; for practitioners and policymakers, these estimates do not support dietary components as a substitute for established treatment or as a stand-alone prevention target.

articles_hidden.title: Looping effects and the cognitive source of epistemic injustices: A simulation study
articles_hidden.authors: Axel Constant; Christophe Gauld; Ana Gomez-Carrillo; Laurence Kirmayer; Karl Friston
articles_hidden.abstract: Patient–clinician interactions are central to diagnosis and treatment in mental health care. They involve inferential processes grounded in patients’ reports of symptoms and clinicians’ interpretations of signs. These processes are liable to microdynamic looping effects that drive diagnostic belief formation. In facing the hermeneutic challenge of reaching a shared ascription of the patient’s condition, such looping effects can lead to misalignment and give rise to epistemic injustice if a credibility deficit exists between the patient and the clinician. In this paper, we use the active inference framework to develop a computational model of looping microdynamics that captures how patients and clinicians reciprocally interpret symptoms, attribute causes, and negotiate diagnostic categories over time. We present a simulation study showing how specific interactional patterns can amplify or mitigate credibility deficits, depending in part on clinicians’ attributional attitudes toward patients’ self-interpretations. Our results suggest that, in contexts of diagnostic disagreement, positive disconfirmation—offering an alternative explanatory framing rather than simply negating the patient’s perspective—may reduce the risk of epistemic injustice. Overall, the model highlights how looping microdynamics structure mutual belief formation in clinical encounters and how attention to these dynamics can support more epistemically responsible clinical communication.

articles_hidden.title: Moral Preferences for Avoiding Non-Lethal Human Injury over Property Damage in Autonomous Vehicle Accidents
articles_hidden.authors: Kiichi INARIMORI; Yuri Tanaka; Takashi Hikasa; Tsutomu Sawai
articles_hidden.abstract: Given the rapid development of autonomous vehicle (AV) technologies, recent studies, such as the Moral Machine Experiment, have examined people’s moral judgments in trolley-style dilemmas, where AVs must choose between unavoidable outcomes, often involving whether to change course to save a greater number of lives. However, fatal injuries represent only a subset of harms caused by traffic agents; most traffic accidents are non-fatal or involve only property damage. The present study focuses on trade-offs between human harm and property damage, examining whether the principle of the priority of human over property (PPHP)—reflected in some ethical and legal guidelines—is consistently supported by the public. Across a series of online experiments, we investigated whether people’s path preferences in scenarios where an AV must choose between avoiding human harm and avoiding property damage align with PPHP. We manipulated several factors, including the severity of harm to the pedestrian, the value of the property, the observer’s perspective (first-person vs. third-person), the gender of the potential victim, and whether the passenger would bear legal liability. The results indicate that participants are more likely to prioritize avoiding property damage when the expected harm to humans is relatively low compared to the value of the property. This tendency is amplified when passengers are held legally liable and among participants with more utilitarian moral attitudes. These findings suggest that AV behavior strictly guided by PPHP is not always supported by lay moral judgments.

articles_hidden.title: Number personification and imaginary companions: Concurrent rather than developmental links in school-age children
articles_hidden.authors: Eiko Matsuda; Acer Yu-Chan Chang; Yusuke Moriguchi; Osamu Sakura
articles_hidden.abstract: Number personification (NP), the attribution of gender, age, or character to digits, is common among 9- to 12-year-olds, but its relationship to other forms of childhood personification remains unknown. Because NP and imaginary companions (ICs) share the attribution of personhood to non-living entities and high idiosyncrasy, we hypothesized that NP is a developmental extension of ICs. In a web survey, 2,193 Japanese mothers of children in grades 1--6 reported their child's current and past IC and NP status and fantasy orientation. Current ICs were reported for 15.1¥% of children, and current NP for 1.2¥%. Contrary to our hypothesis, past IC did not predict current NP; instead, children with a current IC had four times the odds of NP (odds ratio = 4.16). Grade, gender, and fantasy orientation were related to ICs but not, or only weakly, to NP. NP appears to co-occur with ICs rather than to follow them developmentally.

articles_hidden.title: A Computational Approach to Search in Visual Working Memory
articles_hidden.authors: Aditi Singh; Andra Mihali; Wen-Chuang Chou; Wei Ji Ma
articles_hidden.abstract: Search in visual working memory (VWM) is  an important  process in everyday life, but it has so far not been investigated sufficiently using psychophysical and computational approaches. Here, we examine whether computational process models from the study of VWM and of visual search also apply to search in VWM. Participants performed a two-alternative VWM-based color localization task in which set size and color similarity were varied. We tested models with a resource-limited encoding stage and a Bayesian decision stage. We found that a variable-precision model fit the data well and that adding an item limit did not improve the fit. Next, we took a resource-rational approach, in which mean precision at each set size is set by optimizing a combination between behavioral performance and encoding cost. We found that a resource-rational model with an ad-hoc cost function captures behavior well, but not better than the best non-resource-rational model. Our results, albeit unsurprising, contribute to the evidence that search in VWM is very similar to search in perception.

articles_hidden.title: Benchmarking an automated speech recognition pipeline for Spanish-English bilingual preschoolers: Quantifying language input and output in daylong recordings.
articles_hidden.authors: Gaurab Subedi; Marvin Lavechin; Jorge Fonseca; Sarah Surrain
articles_hidden.abstract: Measuring how much of each language bilingual children hear and use in their daily lives requires transcribing long, naturalistic recordings, which is too costly to do by hand at scale. We benchmarked four WhisperX-based automatic speech recognition pipelines, differing in how speech is located and attributed to speakers, against expert transcripts of 168 five-minute clips (14 hours) drawn from daylong home recordings of 14 Spanish--English bilingual preschoolers. Word error rates across pipelines were high (69.5% to 82.0% overall), compared with 35.4% (key child) and 53.9% (adults) between expert coders. Running a child-centered voice type classifier (VTC2) before transcription attributed words to speakers far better than labeling speakers afterwards; we retained this pipeline (WER = 71.4%). Despite word-level errors, it preserved the rank order of clips; automated and manual counts of total and distinct words correlated at r = .83 to .93 for adults and the key child in each language. Agreement rose further at the recording level. Lexical diversity was recovered best: slopes for distinct words (0.79 to 0.88) were closer to one than for total words (0.53 to 0.77). The proportion of Spanish was underestimated (adults: 77% vs. 89%; key child: 70% vs. 90%), largely because WhisperX output short English phrases on brief, unclear audio. Open, inspectable pipelines can yield language-specific measures of bilingual adult input and child output, but precise word counts and language proportions require correction before direct interpretation. These estimates, from one Spanish--English community, will need re-estimating in other populations.

articles_hidden.title: Decisions About Expressing Subjective States Generalise Across Psychological Domain
articles_hidden.authors: Jess Grimmond; Scott Brown; Quentin Frederik Gronau; Guy Hawkins
articles_hidden.abstract:
People routinely make decisions about how to express their internal psychological states to the
outside world. These communication choices can systematically influence the meaning observers
extract about the internal states of others. In psychological science, this is frequently observed in
the way people respond to self-report surveys. Quantitative cognitive models of these
communication choices, such as the Latent State and Response Style (LASARS) model, translate
continuous psychological states into Likert-type responses. In doing so, the model can separate
internal experiences (latent states) from preferences for (or against) certain response options in
self-report scenarios. A key assumption of the LASARS model is that response style reflects a
stable individual characteristic that generalises across contexts. The present study tested this
assumption by examining whether response styles remain consistent across theoretically distinct
psychological domains. A sample of 145 adults completed four survey instruments assessing
sensation seeking, thinking styles, dark personality traits, and perceived control. We compared a
model in which response style parameters were estimated separately for each instrument with a
more parsimonious model in which response style was assumed to be identical across all
instruments. Response style parameters exhibited strong cross-instrument correlations, exceeding
the magnitude of correlations observed among latent states. Furthermore, constraining response
style to be shared across instruments produced virtually identical predictions of observed scores
and latent state estimates while reducing model complexity substantially. These findings provide
strong evidence that response style is a stable, domain-general characteristic. They also support
the conclusion that people use similar decision strategies to express their internal psychological
states across the different constructs they may wish or be asked to communicate.

articles_hidden.title: Comment on Suresh et al. (2026): Drug-level sample size, validation and embedding confounds in receptor–semantic mappings
articles_hidden.authors: Tim Kmecl
articles_hidden.abstract: Suresh et al. (2026, Psychopharmacology) related GloVe embeddings of 4,496 first-hand reports of 21 psychedelic drugs to receptor affinity profiles using partial least squares regression (PLSR), and reported associations between specific receptors and experiential themes. Because affinities vary only between drugs, every report of a drug carries the same profile. I show algebraically that within-drug variation drops out of every cross-product with the affinities. The published loadings can be reproduced from the drug means alone (r ≥ 0.998), so the analysis rests on 21 drugs, with a Kish effective sample size of about 11, rather than on 4,496 reports. The model is near-saturated at the drug level. The cross-validation, receptor subset selection and loading interpretation have not been assessed at the drug level, and the associations have not been tested against chance or for generalisation beyond the few heavily weighted drugs, within the sample or to new ones. A reanalysis of published values shows that the first three components closely follow the DMT–MDMA contrast (r = 0.93), mean report length (r = 0.96) and the LSD–DMT contrast (r = 0.97). The length component follows from summing word vectors. I propose drug-level validation, permutation and resampling analyses that can be run on the existing data. Code reproducing all numbers is publicly available.

articles_hidden.title: Innateness is (still) an orienting principle for language development
articles_hidden.authors: Leher Singh; Marisa Casillas; Shanley E. M. Allen; Michael C. Frank; Caroline F Rowland
articles_hidden.abstract:
How humans come to acquire language has been a persistent object of philosophical and scientific inquiry, in part because it bears on fundamental questions about the nature of human cognition.
Classically, this field of inquiry has centered innateness as a critical component of language acquisition, traditionally characterizing innate capability in terms of richly specified, biologically endowed linguistic structure, such as Universal Grammar. Contemporary theories have evolved considerably from these earlier formulations and now present several differing candidates for innateness in language. Throughout this evolution, though, questions of innateness have remained central to theories of language acquisition, even as the nature of those questions has shifted in response to new sources of evidence. In this Perspective, we consider evidence from three complementary sources of evidence—linguistic diversity, human social interaction, and language models (LMs)—that together inform the question of what children must bring to the task of language learning. We conclude by identifying desiderata for theories of language acquisition that seek to specify the nature, scope, and explanatory role of innate contributions to language development.

articles_hidden.title: A mind-body disconnection? Discordance between thoughts about stress and cardiovascular stress responses
articles_hidden.authors: Audrey Merwin; Brett J. Peters; Elizabeth Haudrich; Abriana M Gresham; Ashley Tudder; Nathan Stuart; Jessica Lang; Kylee Bernel; Parastesh Sattari; Peggy Zoccola
articles_hidden.abstract: Stress responses are defined by mind-body interactions that engage both psychological and physiological processes. We provide foundational research investigating the mind-body connection during stress to ask: how do individuals’ thoughts about stressors align with their cardiovascular responses? 925 dyads (N = 1,850) anticipated, engaged in, and recovered from stress-inducing social-evaluative tasks. Analyses revealed that individuals’ self-reported and cardiovascular indices of stress were not significantly associated at any timepoint, bolstered by post-hoc Inclusion Bayes Factors supporting the null (vs. alternative) hypothesis. Meta-analytic results suggested the association between measures is effectively zero, indicating findings may generalize beyond a social interaction context and our primarily White, female, college-aged sample. These findings suggest individuals’ perceptions of stress may be distinct from their physiological stress responses, carry significant implications for the way we conceptualize and measure stress, and indicate that multi-method, full-body approaches are critical for a holistic understanding of the human stress response.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting the Radius of Trust Problem: Who Counts as “Most People”?
articles_hidden.authors: Anu Realo; Jüri Allik
articles_hidden.abstract: General trust in social surveys is usually measured with a Single-Item General Trust (SIGT) question that asks whether “most people” can be trusted. The concept of the radius of trust challenges this approach by highlighting that trust may vary with the social distance between those who express trust and those who are trusted. This has led to the addition of six specific trust questions to the World Values Survey (WVS) questionnaire since Wave 5, which ask respondents to rate their trust in their family, neighborhood, and people they know personally, as well as in people of another religion, people of another nationality, and people they meet for the first time. Analyzing respondents’ answers to the SIGT and six specific trust items in the Integrated Values Surveys (IVS) dataset (1981-2022) across 88 countries and territories and the three most recent survey waves, we find that trust is a complex construct whose invariant property across cultures is a fixed-length vector composed of the squares of its two components: ingroup and outgroup trust. The phrase “most people” in the SIGT question appears to refer to “familiar strangers”—people whom respondents do not know personally but are likely to encounter in everyday life. It is trust in these familiar strangers, rather than in more distant outgroups, which is most strongly associated with the Human Development Index. This association, however, becomes pronounced only at very high levels of human development.

articles_hidden.title: Distinct sensorimotor representations during combined action observation and motor imagery
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew Scott; David Wright; Nicola Jane Hodges; Justine Magnuson; Sarah N Kraeutner
articles_hidden.abstract: The human sensorimotor system can represent actions in the absence of movement, termed motor simulation. These motor simulations can be perceptually (externally) driven through observation of an actor or cognitively (internally) driven through imagining movement. Although there is evidence humans can represent multiple actions simultaneously, whether different motor simulations can concurrently be represented is unclear. We investigated the capacity of the sensorimotor system to simultaneously represent observed (action observation; AO) and imagined actions (motor imagery; MI). Two competing hypotheses were tested concerning whether AO and MI could co-exist or not, The Dual Action Simulation Hypothesis (DASH) and Visual Guidance Hypothesis (VGH), respectively. Fifteen participants completed a functional magnetic resonance imagining (fMRI) study, requiring them to complete four distinct conditions involving imagination or observation of a rhythmical hand tapping action. Conditions involved: AO, AO with a counting task (i.e., with cognitive load), MI, or simultaneous AO and MI of different actions (AOMI). Through representational similarity analysis, AO and MI motor simulations were evidenced in the right ventral premotor cortex, supporting DASH over VGH. Multidimensional scaling of representational similarity data indicated a unique representational pattern for AOMI, differing from AO and MI across different dimensions. Whole-brain analyses were conducted, showing descriptive support for greater engagement of sensorimotor regions during AOMI vs. the summation of independent AO and MI conditions occurred, complementing findings from our representational similarity analysis. While dual motor simulations appear possible, our data suggests that the representational pattern of AOMI is distinct, producing super-additive sensorimotor activity. Neither DASH nor VGH adequately explain these data.

articles_hidden.title: Disasters and Sports in Dreams: Unexpected Selectivity in Dream Incorporation
articles_hidden.authors: Marcin Florkowski
articles_hidden.abstract:
